articles.title: What happens if Democrats take Congress? Trump’s power explained
articles.summary: Democrats could regain subpoena power and committee control, but they wouldn't have free rein to enact their agenda.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With Republicans currently holding control of the House and Senate, the midterm elections could bring changes that affect the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate. They also control the House, with 218 seats to Democrats' 214.

With Trump's approval rating at the lowest level of his presidency , the election could reshape Washington. Yet even if Democrats win one or both chambers, Trump would retain veto power and broad executive authority, limiting Democrats' ability to enact major legislation.

If Democrats win both the House and Senate, it would significantly change how Washington operates during the final two years of Trump's presidency.

The biggest change would be Democrats regaining control of Congress and shifting power in Washington. That would allow them to block much of Trump's legislative agenda, investigate his administration and determine which bills reach his desk.

However, any major Democratic legislation passed by both chambers would still require Trump's signature to become law.

Could a Democratic sweep turn Trump into a lame duck early?

If Democrats win both the House and Senate, Trump could become a lame-duck president. A lame duck is a president whose political influence has weakened, often because they are nearing the end of their term or losing the ability to advance their agenda.

If Democrats win the House, they would gain control of House committees, subpoena power and the authority to investigate Trump and his administration, Reuters reported . Trump administration officials could be targeted by congressional subpoenas, though they could defy them because a Justice Department led by Trump appointees would be unlikely to enforce them.

Trump would still retain veto power and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and foreign policy. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Oct. 20 there would be " very little " a Democratic-controlled House could do to block Trump's agenda.

A greater impact would come if Democrats win both the House and Senate. Democrats would take control of Senate committees and the chamber's agenda. They would likely block many of Trump's judicial nominees and could seek to delay filling any U.S. Supreme Court vacancy until after the 2028 presidential election.

Trump, however, would still retain veto power and executive authority. Major legislation would remain difficult to pass because most bills require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, the Senate rule that allows the minority party to block or delay legislation.

articles.title: Byron Donalds Offers Florida More of the MAGA Same in Governor's Race
articles.summary: Donalds is long on promises, short on details, and still trying to sell Ron DeSantis' culture war.
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds' (R–Fla.) closing pitch to voters in his campaign for Florida governor is the same one he's relied on his whole political career: success through affiliation. If you like President Donald Trump and current Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Donalds promises, you'll like him.

"The Democrats are now arguing that they want change," Donalds said at a campaign event on Sunday in Tampa. "And I look at my opponent. I look at these Democrats that are running, and I say to myself, 'Change what?' We are the best state in America."

If he wins on Tuesday, Donalds will have gone from a backbench congressman to Florida's first black governor in roughly six years, inheriting an office that has swelled in power under DeSantis. With the help of an acquiescent GOP-controlled state legislature and litigious state attorney general, DeSantis became the most powerful Florida governor in living memory.

Donalds doesn't offer detailed plans about what he would do with that accumulated power, but judging from his campaign speeches and statements, it would presumably be a continuation of DeSantis' heavy-handed brand of top-down conservative government.

"Florida hasn't happened by accident," Donalds said in a Fox Business interview last Wednesday. "This is something that has been about consistent leadership over time in our state. Gov. DeSantis has done a great job."

"It's about reminding voters that you have to choose for Florida to continue to be the free state of Florida," he continued.

Voters usually don't have to be reminded when things are going well, though. That might be partly why Donalds is in a tighter-than-expected race against Democratic candidate David Jolly.

A Stetson University poll released on October 30 found Donalds leading Jolly 51 percent to 45 percent, but also found that statewide Republican candidates' margins were roughly half of what pollsters measured in mid-October. It would still be a shocking upset if Florida Republicans lose any statewide races, but the trend is a warning sign for a Florida GOP that has made significant gains against Democrats for the past several election cycles in a row.

In addition to national pessimism over the economy and direction of the country, Donalds is being dragged down by a state political legacy that is several years past its sell-by date.

In many cases, DeSantis' efforts to make Florida the tip of the spear of the national conservative movement have, rather than expanding freedom, fed a growing police state : The state launched overbroad reviews of school library catalogs, monitored and threatened drag shows , enacted anti-competitive bans on lab-grown meat , and crusaded to stop cities from painting rainbows on their crosswalks. Florida's culture war bills have, in many cases, been expensive failures. Judges struck down Florida's ban on social media for children under 14 and large portions of the state's Individual Freedom Act of 2022, better known as the "Stop WOKE Act."

In his August 18 victory speech after winning the Republican gubernatorial primary, Donalds said his goal is to preserve "the Florida dream," which he says under former Republicans Gov. Charlie Christ and DeSantis have become "the envy of every state of America."

Donalds' campaign website and stump speeches offer few concrete details on how he would do this. He promises to make Florida "accountable, achievable and affordable." (One is tempted to ask why, after two years of a "golden age" under Trump and six years of freedom under DeSantis, Floridians' primary concern is affordability.)

Donalds promises every state contract, budget, and fee will be posted publicly. "Taxpayers deserve to know that their hard-earned dollars are being spent efficiently, transparently, and with absolute integrity," he said at his victory speech.

Donalds is correct, but the DeSantis administration would be a terrible example to follow. DeSantis spent more than $1 billion building and operating the "Alligator Alcatraz" detention camp, removed the contracts from a public database, and then closed the camp less than a year later. Another of DeSantis' major projects over the course of his terms has been gutting Florida's once-strong public records law .

As for fiscal responsibility, Donalds said his administration would continue the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative started under DeSantis. "We are going to DOGE every agency," Donalds said. "There will be no sacred cows."

A short while later, after name-checking several Florida sheriffs in the audience, Donalds also said, "We will not jeopardize funding for police, firefighters, and first responders."

Donalds also promises to "slash red tape" by streamlining government permitting and decrease costs to consumers by forcing hospitals and insurance companies to provide transparent billing.

Among the issues where Donalds aligns with libertarian values is his staunch support of school choice and the Second Amendment. Donalds' wife runs a network of charter schools, which have been the subject of media investigations since Donalds announced his candidacy.

But if Donalds' voting record in Congress is an indication of his leadership, it is not reassuring. Donalds voted multiple times against nonbinding war powers resolutions to require Trump to cease hostilities with Iran ("All you're doing is providing more leverage to the Iranian regime," Donalds said of the resolutions), voted for the fiscally ruinous One Big, Beautiful Bill Act , and voted against certifying 2020 election results—none of which speak well of how seriously he takes the role of Congress or his job as a member of it.

Donalds' rhetoric about affordability and transparency would be more convincing if he were honest with voters about the excesses of his predecessor, or at least not enthusiastic about them. Florida's next governor must commit to truly rebuilding transparency and accountability in the state government, and that will require more than just the same old reheated MAGA leftovers.

articles.body:
Daniel Vorcaro, ex-banqueiro do Master, em depoimento à PF no dia 15 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: Reprodução

A defesa de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, aposta na perícia para sustentar sua estratégia de tentar anular investigações, enquanto a possibilidade de uma delação premiada fica cada vez mais distante.

articles.title: Fux cita críticas nas redes e diz que STF já discutiu consequências nocivas das bets | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro afirmou ser contrário às bets, mas disse que a análise da MP envolve novos argumentos e depende do colegiado do STF.
articles.summary: Ministro afirmou ser contrário às bets, mas disse que a análise da MP envolve novos argumentos e depende do colegiado do STF.
articles.body:
O ministro Luiz Fux , do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), afirmou nesta terça-feira (3), na abertura de uma audiência pública sobre as bets, que a Corte já discutiu as consequências nocivas das apostas em audiências anteriores.

O ministro disse que decidiu fazer o esclarecimento diante de “algumas manifestações das redes”.

A declaração ocorre no mesmo dia em que o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) pediu, em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais, que a sociedade civil acompanhe a audiência e participe do debate “para que haja justiça na decisão”.

“Eu gostaria inicialmente de fazer alguns esclarecimentos que talvez não sejam do conhecimento do público em geral. Aliás, mostrou-se não ser mesmo do conhecimento do público em geral, tendo em vista algumas manifestações das redes”, afirmou Fux.

O ministro relembrou audiências realizadas em novembro de 2024 sobre a legislação que autorizou e regulamentou o mercado de apostas.

Segundo Fux, naquelas audiências foram “amplamente discutidas as consequências nocivas” das bets.

Na sequência, Fux afirmou que os debates anteriores abordaram consequências psíquicas e sociais das apostas.

O ministro mencionou ainda entidades ouvidas à época e afirmou que foram apresentados dados sobre o transtorno do jogo.

🔎 A ludopatia, também chamada de transtorno do jogo, é uma condição médica caracterizada pelo desejo incontrolável de continuar jogando ou apostando. Ela é reconhecida como doença pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS).

Ao falar de forma geral sobre as bets, o ministro disse que sua “percepção” é de que elas “devem ser banidas”.

Fux ressaltou, porém, que essa avaliação não encerra a análise das ações sobre a medida provisória , que envolve outros argumentos e depende do colegiado do STF.

Fux rebateu ainda críticas à composição da audiência. “Não procede alegação de que eu só convoquei empresas e times de futebol”, afirmou. Ele citou, entre os convidados, a Associação Brasileira de Supermercados e o ministro da Justiça.

Fux afirmou que a edição da medida provisória trouxe novas questões que precisarão ser examinadas pelo STF. Entre elas, citou segurança jurídica, aplicação da lei a atos anteriores, proteção da confiança de empresas autorizadas a operar e se estavam presentes as condições de relevância e urgência exigidas para a edição de uma medida provisória.

“Eu vou reiterar, evidentemente, os meus argumentos que eu utilizei com relação aos jogos de azar em geral e também vou levar os novos argumentos que surgiram em razão da medida provisória”, afirmou.

Ministro Luiz Fux durante julgamento no Supremo — Foto: Luiz Silveira/STF

Antes da audiência desta terça, Lula publicou um vídeo nas redes sociais no qual pediu participação da sociedade civil na discussão.

“É importante que a sociedade civil participe para que haja justiça na decisão”, afirmou o presidente.

Lula também voltou a associar as apostas ao sofrimento das famílias pobres e defendeu que as bets continuem proibidas.

A posição repete argumentos apresentados pelo presidente ao anunciar a proibição, em 25 de setembro. Na ocasião, Lula afirmou ter decidido tomar uma medida “dura e drástica” para acabar com as bets.

Fux é relator dos pedidos apresentados pela Associação Nacional de Jogos e Loterias (ANJL) e pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Jogo Responsável (IBJR) contra a medida provisória que proibiu as bets.

As duas entidades pediram ao Supremo a suspensão dos efeitos da MP e a manutenção do funcionamento das empresas que estavam autorizadas a operar.

Entre os argumentos, afirmam que a interrupção das atividades viola a segurança jurídica e pode provocar a migração de apostadores para o mercado clandestino.

O governo defende a manutenção da proibição. A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) afirmou ao STF que há razões econômicas, sociais e de saúde para a medida. O órgão também sugeriu a Fux que avaliasse a realização de uma nova audiência pública.

Na audiência desta terça, dois ministros do governo defenderam a medida. O ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Wellington César Lima e Silva, afirmou que o governo buscou ouvir os setores envolvidos e evitar uma proibição que produzisse efeitos indesejáveis, mas concluiu que era necessário agir diante dos impactos das apostas sobre indivíduos e famílias.

Wellington César Lima e Silva disse defender uma atividade econômica “pujante”, mas afirmou que ela não pode se desenvolver com a “vitimização” de pessoas que, segundo ele, estão em desvantagem diante dos mecanismos tecnológicos utilizados pelas plataformas.

Já o advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias, concentrou a exposição nos argumentos jurídicos. Ele afirmou que a União considera a MP constitucional e defende que ela seja integralmente preservada.

Segundo Jorge Messias, o governo entende que o Estado pode e deve intervir em uma atividade econômica quando os mecanismos de proteção se mostram insuficientes para preservar direitos fundamentais.

O advogado-geral afirmou ainda que, para a União, a urgência da MP decorre da continuidade dos danos provocados pelas apostas e da necessidade de impedir que eles se ampliem.

Jorge Messias reconheceu a importância da segurança jurídica, mas disse que questões patrimoniais das empresas não garantem o direito à manutenção do regime de exploração das apostas.

Representantes de time de futebol como o Flamengo, Fluminense e Botafogo criticaram a proibição imediata das bets e afirmaram que a medida compromete receitas e contratos que haviam sido planejados com base na regulamentação anterior.

Os clubes defenderam um período maior de transição e regras mais rígidas para o setor como alternativa à proibição total.

Pelo Flamengo, o representante afirmou que o clube assumiu compromissos financeiros com atletas e empregados contando com as receitas dos contratos de patrocínio e defendeu que eles sejam protegidos.

“O Flamengo se organizou financeiramente para os próximos quatro, cinco anos com base no contrato assinado, de acordo com a legislação vigente”, disse.

O Fluminense destacou que os efeitos não se restringem aos grandes clubes. Segundo o representante, equipes menores e times da Série B já enfrentam redução nas propostas por direitos de transmissão.

Ele criticou especialmente o prazo de transição previsto para a publicidade das bets e comparou o Brasil com outros países: “Bélgica, 56 meses de período de transição; Reino Unido, 36 meses; Espanha, 12 meses; Itália, 10 meses; Brasil, 10 dias”.

O representante do Fluminense também contrapôs o argumento do governo sobre os efeitos sociais das apostas ao impacto econômico da proibição sobre o futebol: “O drama de uma família endividada não pode ser maior do que o drama de uma família que vai ter que sofrer os efeitos do desemprego”.

Já o Botafogo afirmou que perdeu, com a proibição, o maior patrocínio da história do clube e disse que os recursos também financiavam as categorias de base e o futebol feminino. O representante afirmou ainda que o plano de recuperação judicial do clube contava com o fluxo de caixa do contrato com a empresa de apostas.

O Botafogo também criticou o prazo para adaptação. Segundo o representante, os dez dias previstos não foram “adequados ou minimamente suficientes” e a receita perdida desde a entrada em vigor da proibição não será recuperada mesmo que os efeitos da MP venham a ser suspensos.

Representantes de Cruzeiro e São Paulo também criticaram a proibição. Pelo Cruzeiro, José Francisco Cimino Manssur afirmou considerar a medida ineficaz e argumentou que a proibição da publicidade de casas de apostas pode criar um desequilíbrio entre clubes brasileiros e equipes estrangeiras que disputam partidas no país exibindo marcas do setor.

“Eu acredito que a proibição seja ineficaz”, afirmou José Francisco Cimino Manssur.

Pelo São Paulo, Danielle Maiolini Mendes afirmou que a proibição não impede que plataformas ilegais continuem usando jogos, clubes e atletas brasileiros como objeto de apostas e argumentou que empresas do mercado regulado auxiliavam no compartilhamento de informações para combater a manipulação de competições.

Ela afirmou ainda que o clube tem contrato de patrocínio com vigência até 2030 e que essa receita faz parte do planejamento do futebol profissional, das categorias de base e do futebol feminino.

O Corinthians também defendeu um período de transição. O representante do clube afirmou que a suspensão abrupta das receitas pode aumentar a diferença financeira em relação a equipes de países vizinhos que continuam autorizadas a receber patrocínio de empresas de apostas.

“Tem que ocorrer a modulação, tem que ocorrer um período de transição, tem que ocorrer uma adequação. O que não pode é, de um momento para o outro, isso ser cerceado do clube de futebol”, afirmou o representante do Corinthians.

Representantes dos atletas profissionais também pediram que o STF considere os efeitos da proibição sobre o emprego no futebol.

Segundo Murilo Aragão, grandes clubes têm maior capacidade de substituir receitas por causa da força de suas marcas, mas equipes menores podem ter mais dificuldade para absorver a perda dos recursos das bets.

“Os nossos pleitos, como amigo da Corte, são que o efeito da medida provisória em questão considere o efeito no emprego dos atletas no país”, afirmou Aragão.

Em 2025, as bets pagaram R$ 1,143 bilhão em patrocínios aos 20 clubes brasileiros de maior receita, o equivalente a cerca de 36% das receitas de marketing desses times.

A proibição foi determinada por uma medida provisória publicada em 25 de setembro. A norma proibiu a exploração, a oferta, a intermediação e a publicidade das apostas de quota fixa no Brasil.

articles.title: Bolsonaro articula eleição do Senado de olho em anistia | G1
articles.standfirst: Possível acordo incluiria apoio à reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre para o comando da Casa.
articles.summary: Possível acordo incluiria apoio à reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre para o comando da Casa.
articles.body:
O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro( PL ) acompanha de perto e tenta influenciar as articulações da direita para a eleição da presidência do Senado .

O objetivo principal é garantir uma anistia que o livre de cumprir a pena de 27 anos de prisão à qual foi condenado por tentar um golpe de Estado.

Segundo setores do PL, nessa conta pode entrar até um eventual apoio à reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), mesmo que isso signifique sacrificar apoio à candidatura do aliado Rogério Marinho (PL-RN).

A avaliação é que, para Bolsonaro, a anistia se sobrepõe aos interesses eleitorais do próprio partido.

Há setores do bolsonarismo em conversas com a esquerda para que haja algum acordo nesse sentido.

Mesmo que seja jogo combinado de discurso para dizer que não topam a anistia, mas não fazerem força para vetar o acordo.

Assim, garantiriam Alcolumbre na presidência do Senado — que é o desejo do Palácio do Planalto.

Plenário do Senado Federal — Foto: Jonas Pereira/Agência Senado

articles.title: Passagem de ônibus em Prudente sobe para R$ 6 em meio a reclamações | G1
articles.standfirst: Reajuste de R$ 1 entrou em vigor no domingo (1º); usuários relatam espera de até uma hora nos pontos e pedem melhorias no transporte coletivo.
articles.summary: A passagem de ônibus em Presidente Prudente subiu para R$ 6 após três anos. Usuários cobram melhorias no serviço da SOU Prudente e reclamam da demora nos pontos.
articles.body:
O reajuste da tarifa do ônibus para R$ 6,00 em Presidente Prudente (SP) foi recebido por usuários com reclamações e cobrança por melhorias. Passageiros ouvidos pela TV TEM nesta terça-feira (3) reivindicam mais horários e mais veículos para diminuir o tempo de espera nos pontos, que em alguns casos chega a uma hora.

O novo valor entrou em vigor no domingo (1º), autorizado pelo Decreto nº 38.327, publicado pela Prefeitura de Prudente em 21 de outubro , no Diário Oficial do Município. Houve acréscimo de R$ 1 em relação à tarifa anterior.

De acordo com o documento, a tarifa estava sem reajuste desde janeiro de 2023. A prefeitura afirmou ter destinado aproximadamente R$ 54 milhões em subsídios para cobrir os custos do sistema de transporte público e manter o valor pago pelos passageiros, durante esses quase três anos.

Diante do reajuste da tarifa para R$ 6,00 em Presidente Prudente (SP), passageiros reclamam da demora entre ônibus e da qualidade do serviço — Foto: Emerson Sanchez/TV TEM

Diante do aumento da tarifa, os passageiros cobram melhorias no transporte coletivo. Para a empregada doméstica Madalena Damasceno, um dos principais problemas é a demora entre um ônibus e outro.

“Demora muito para passar no ponto. É de hora em hora”, disse à TV TEM , enquanto esperava por ônibus, na manhã desta terça-feira.

O vendedor Adrian Souza, que também reclama da quantidade de ônibus à disposição dos passageiros, espera que o serviço melhor a partir do reajuste.

“Tomara que melhore o transporte, que aumente (a quantidade) de ônibus. Com cinco reais, já era caro. Imagina agora com seis reais (a passagem”, declarou, à TV TEM .

O estagiário Caio Henrique Araújo também reclamou do reajuste e da qualidade do transporte coletivo. “Espero que o reajuste reflita em melhoria na nossa experiência como usuário, porque vai pesar no bolso no final do mês”, disse ele.

Ônibus circula em Presidente Prudente (SP) com nova tarifa, de R$ 6,00, em vigor: passageiros reclamam do reajuste e da qualidade do serviço — Foto: Emerson Sanchez/TV TEM

O serviço de transporte coletivo em Presidente Prudente é prestado pela concessionária Sancetur Santa Cecília Turismo Ltda., conhecida pelo nome de SOU Prudente.

Para justificar o reajuste da tarifa, a Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade Urbana (Semob) citou que o valor estava sem reajuste há três anos , período em que houve aumento de custos operacionais, como combustíveis, salários, encargos trabalhistas, pneus, peças, manutenção e seguros.

De acordo com a pasta, a tarifa técnica, que corresponde ao custo efetivo do serviço, é de aproximadamente R$ 15,23 por passageiro. Com a passagem fixada em R$ 6, o usuário pagará cerca de 39% desse valor, enquanto a diferença, superior a R$ 9 por passageiro, continuará sendo coberta por subsídios municipais e outras fontes de custeio.

A atualização tarifária também ocorre após questionamentos do Ministério Público do Estado de São Paulo (MP-SP), que solicitou esclarecimentos sobre a ausência de reajuste anual, os motivos para a manutenção do valor e a situação financeira do sistema.

articles.title: PEC da Segurança Pública: Lula enfrenta 1º teste no Congresso | G1
articles.standfirst: Planalto tenta aprovar proposta no Senado em dois turnos, enquanto oposição articula obstrução e redução da maioridade penal para 14 anos em caso de crimes hediondos.
articles.summary: A votação da PEC da Segurança Pública no Senado nesta terça-feira define a recriação de ministério e mede a força de Lula para o quarto mandato.
articles.body:
A votação da PEC da Segurança Pública vai ser o primeiro teste para o presidente Lula no Congresso, depois de o petista ser reeleito para um quarto mandato. A proposta está agendada para análise nesta terça-feira (3) no Senado .

Lula conta com a aprovação da PEC em dois turnos nesta terça para recriar o Ministério da Segurança Pública e melhorar o combate ao crime organizado no país, um dos pontos fracos dos seus três mandatos à frente do Palácio do Planalto.

O presidente terá um desafio maior no Senado , a partir do próximo ano, diante do tamanho da bancada do PL em 2027, que terá 28 senadores .

Mas, se vencer nesta terça, a aprovação da PEC mostrará que o governo poderá contar com os votos dos demais partidos e, até mesmo, com dissidências no PL , partido do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

Por sinal, a oposição bolsonarista quer derrotar o presidente Lula já de largada, com a atual composição do Senado, e barrar a votação da PEC da Segurança Pública.

Ou aprovar, ao mesmo tempo, uma emenda que reduza a maioridade penal para 16 anos, em casos menos graves, e para 14 anos, nos casos de crimes hediondos.

A votação será também um teste para a escolha do novo presidente do Senado. O atual, Davi Alcolumbre , quer se reeleger, no eleição interna de fevereiro de 2027.

O PL deve lançar oficialmente nesta quarta-feira (4) a candidatura do senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN). A senadora Tereza Cristina (MS) também deve lançar sua candidatura, apesar de seu partido, o PP, já ter anunciado apoio à reeleição de Alcolumbre.

Alcolumbre pode sair fortalecido para a disputa se conseguir aprovar, em dois turnos, a PEC da Segurança Pública nesta terça, da forma como o governo deseja, deixando o tema da maioridade penal para ser analisado, inicialmente, pela Câmara dos Deputados .

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que venceu o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais do Brasil — Foto: REUTERS/Adriano Machado

articles.title: South Carolina Senate race gets unexpectedly close after Lindsey Graham's sister Darline stumbles
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Six months ago, the South Carolina U. Senate race was expected to be another straightforward campaign for incumbent Lindsey Graham and his...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Six months ago, the South Carolina U.S. Senate race was expected to be another straightforward campaign for incumbent Lindsey Graham and his dominant Republican Party.

But Graham's sudden death in July and the elevation of his political neophyte sister Darline from a placeholder role to seeking her own six-year term have roiled the race.

Now supporters of Democrat Annie Andrews can envision something that seemed impossible in this century of double-digit Republican wins — flipping a Senate seat in one of the nation's most reliable GOP strongholds.

Whoever wins will be the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate. But that bit of history has taken a backseat to whispers that have grown into actual predictions that Andrews could be the first Democrat since 1998 to win a statewide race for the U.S. Senate or the governor's office.

Darline Graham went from political sibling to stand-in senator

Darline Graham, by her own admission, is a reluctant candidate. She was abruptly thrust into the political spotlight after her brother, a U.S. Senate stalwart, died seeking his fifth term.

Republican Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to finish her brother's term in a widely hailed move, given the siblings' close relationship. Lindsey Graham helped raise his younger sister after their parents' early deaths.

Darline Graham's decision to seek a full six-year term was more surprising. The snap primary, organized just a month after Lindsey Graham's death, drew some of the top names in South Carolina politics.

President Donald Trump wanted Darline Graham in the Senate, and he immediately and forcefully backed her. The president had feuded with her brother at times but saw Lindsey Graham as an ally during his second White House term, particularly on the war with Iran.

As Darline Graham and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, an occasional Trump critic, battled it out in a primary runoff, the president campaigned for her in the state and returned twice in the final weeks before the election.

But that presidential backing may be eroding Graham's support from both sides. It bothers independent voters unhappy with Trump's second term and Norman supporters on the right who are unhappy that the president interfered in what should be a decision left up to the state's voters. Both groups are uneasy about Graham's inexperience and the prospect of turning the seat into a Graham family dynasty.

In a primary debate, Graham was asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea — a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations. She struggled to answer before admitting, "National security is not my thing."

As Republican-affiliated groups across the country reshuffled last-minute campaign spending, Senate Republicans' primary super PAC sent reinforcements to deep-red South Carolina to shore up Graham , even as Republicans said they remained confident they would retain the seat.

Annie Andrews retooled her campaign to face Darline Graham

Andrews had already been campaigning for more than a year and had won her primary outright when Lindsey Graham died, forcing her to rejigger a general election plan centered on ousting the incumbent.

Andrews has benefited from South Carolina's leadoff status on Democrats' 2028 presidential nominating calendar. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly have visited the state, boosting her visibility and their own.

But in recent weeks, Andrews has run an independent campaign and has rarely appeared alongside prominent Democrats from South Carolina or elsewhere. She has focused on economic problems and says Graham will be like her brother, a part of the same Washington cabal that enriches only itself and cares little about the people back home.

When they met for their sole debate last month , Graham and Andrews traded barbs over the economy, war with Iran and artificial intelligence. But they mostly argued over who was less qualified for the South Carolina Senate seat. Andrews came up short in a 2022 challenge to Rep. Nancy Mace but has remained visible since, though she's never held office or run statewide.

Graham fended off Andrews' accusation that the Republican was seeking to ride her brother's political coattails, saying she had legally kept her maiden name to maintain a connection to her parents, both of whom died when she was young. "Thank you for bringing up a horrible, tragic memory for me," she added.

It's been decades since South Carolina elected a Democrat to the US Senate

A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in October appeared to show a close race.

But polls also showed an apparently close race in 2020, when Lindsey Graham, Democrat Jaime Harrison and outside groups supporting their campaigns spent hundreds of millions of dollars in South Carolina's most expensive election. In that reelection, Lindsey Graham's last, the Republican sailed back into office by a 10-percentage-point margin.

The last Democrat elected to a Senate seat in South Carolina was Fritz Hollings, who won his final term in 1998. Since then, Republicans have held both Senate seats, and only one Democrat — Jim Clyburn — represents the state in the U.S. House.

Republicans have benefited from straight-ticket voting, which allows voters to choose all GOP candidates on their ballot. The race for South Carolina's open governor's seat hasn't appeared as close as the U.S. Senate contest.

Libertarian and Constitution Party candidates are also on the general election ballot.

Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

articles.title: When will we know who won the US midterms?
articles.summary: Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks
articles.body:
Millions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.

Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.

When will we know the results and who controls Congress?

Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.

To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.

First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT) . They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).

Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.

There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine , where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) . These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.

Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.

This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.

The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.

In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.

While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.

The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.

Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days . The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.

Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.

The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat .

Follow live updates on US midterm elections

What are the key races to watch in 2026?

There are six Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report - Alaska , Kansas , Iowa , Maine , Ohio and Texas .

Of these, six are currently held by Republicans. The Democrats would need to win three of those seats, plus five classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

Polls have suggested Democrats have a chance in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

Democrats also need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan , where Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent in a closely-observed race. The state was initially classified as a "toss-up" by Cook Political Report, but was reclassified as "leans Democrat" the day before the vote.

The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.

Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.

The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT) , which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.

Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT) , the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the key battleground states:

19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio , where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold

20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Kansas and Texas

21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa , as well as in Kansas and Texas . In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats

01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska , the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot

Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.

Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.

Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.

Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.

Every state and locality has rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, including how partisan observers can watch the count and, in some states, raise formal challenges.

Tight races will take longer, and create the possibility of recounts being triggered and legal challenges.

Mail-in ballots take longer to count, as officials need to process envelopes and verify signatures.

More than 30 states allow ballots to be processed before election day, but other states do not. In California, all ballots must be posted before or on election day and will still be counted if they arrive within seven days of the election.

In Alaska, ranked-choice voting could mean that tabulations take considerably longer than elsewhere in the country and the controversy over ballots could mean that legal challenges can complicate things.

Once every vote has been included in the final results, and after processes such as recounts have been completed, the election results are certified - first at the local, county, level and then state-wide.

The governor then typically signs the certifications for House and Senate winners to be sent to Congress.

Results can be challenged. Recounts can be requested by candidates in close races, and in some states recounts are automatically triggered if they fall within a certain margin.

Candidates can also file legal election contests alleging irregularities.

Congress has the final word. Losing candidates in both House and Senate races can file contests, with slightly different processes in each of the two chambers.

Both chambers can, theoretically, refuse to seat someone or order an investigation.

Outgoing members of Congress leave office on Sunday 3 January. Because that date falls on a weekend, the new members may take office on the same date unless Congress passes a law setting a different day.

Additional reporting by James FitzGerald, Yazmina García-Fernández, Tom Geoghegan and Mike Hills.

articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Republican Ken Paxton faces off against Democrat James Talarico in the race to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate.

The winner will replace Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton beat out in a runoff in May.

Paxton is endorsed by President Donald Trump and strongly aligns his mission with the president's. He states he will work alongside Trump to take on Big Pharma and Big Food, finish the border wall, focus on national sovereignty and advance an America First foreign policy.

NewsNation provides comprehensive coverage of the 2026 midterm elections like never before, with live results powered by Decision Desk HQ and expert analysis. Stay tuned for race calls after the polls close Tuesday night.

Talarico, a Texas House representative, centers his campaign on serving working people over corporations, lowering healthcare costs and boosting public education. He identifies himself as anti-corruption and points to billionaires, stating on his campaign website that the biggest divide in this country is not right vs. left but top vs. bottom.

Paxton has gone after Talarico's stances, including his recent statement on gender reassignment surgery. Talarico said in an interview he opposes such surgeries for minors.

"This is just the latest example of Talarico masquerading as a moderate when the truth is he's the most radical Democrat to ever run statewide in Texas history," Paxton stated in a news release, according to the El Paso Times.

As the race has heated up, several public figures have raised alarms about each candidate, with President Trump stating on Truth Social that Talarico "may be the worst candidate I have ever seen."

Attorney Dan Cogdell, who defended Paxton when he was impeached in 2023 during his time as Texas attorney general, has since stated that Paxton "has lost sight of his core mission which is to represent the people of Texas."

The attorney went on to endorse Talarico, stating that "unlike Ken, I believe to my core that James Talarico believes in unity over division."

articles.title: Control of Congress up for grabs on Election Day 2026: Live updates
articles.summary: Republicans and Dems are pitching the election as the most important in a generation. At stake is control of Congress for the rest of Trump’s term.
articles.body:
Polling places are opening across the nation Tuesday for the midterm elections that President Donald Trump has called the most important of " our lifetime ."

At stake is control of Congress and whether Trump will finish his final term with Republican majorities in the House and Senate, or Democrats will win enough seats to block an agenda they call dangerous.

"With your vote we will decide: These extremists will be given power or not power," Trump said Monday in a final pitch to voters. "We'll defend our country, our culture, and our heritage for generations to come."

‘I voted’ stickers show unique election pride at midterm polls

Democrats have also pitched the stakes as existential, warning that Trump threatens to crater the American economy with his war on Iran and undermine democracy in the nation with his aggressive immigration enforcement agenda.

"We've seen in these last few months attacks on civil rights and voting rights unprecedented for decades," Sen. Jon Ossoff on Monday told supporters in Georgia, where he faces reelection. "But when our civil rights and voting rights are under attack, we defend them by using them."

Bookmark these pages to follow Tuesday's official results : U.S. House Election Results | U.S. Senate Election Results

Husted says only poll that counts is Election Day

11:07 AM ET, November 3 2026, Bart Jansen

Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to succeed Vice President JD Vance, told reporters after voting that he didn't have any opinion about polls showing him trailing Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

"The only poll that matters is the one that's being taken today for real by the voters of this state," Husted said. "I hope to win and I hope to live up to the expectations that people have of me."

Contingency plans will help voters cast ballots despite severe weather

10:59 AM ET, November 3 2026, Erin Mansfield

Karen Brinson Bell, the founder and co-lead of the Partnership for Elections & Emergency Response, urged voters affected by severe weather to check their official state and local election office websites for the latest information on voting.

"Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah have all faced flooding and evacuations in parts of those states as a severe storm system moved through yesterday and continues across the country today," Bell told USA TODAY.

"A tornado was reported in Oklahoma," Bell added. "Kansas and Tennessee are facing strong winds and other severe weather conditions from this system. A separate storm system caused flooding in Florida."

"In response, election officials have done what they always do – they have worked their contingency plans and voting continues," Bell said. "Several states have declared emergencies which provide additional measures to allow voters to cast their ballots."

Trump claims fraud in Alaska senate race

10:47 AM ET, November 3 2026, Trevor Hughes

Trump continues to highlight what he calls fraud in the Alaska Senate race, based on two candidates having virtually identical names.

The New York Times last month reported that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had been recruited into the race by Democratic activists. The incumbent is Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, and the GOP complains that having two Sullivans on Alaska's ballot might confuse voters enough to give Democrat Mary Peltola an advantage in the state's ranked-choice voting system.

The president, in a late-night social media post before Election Day, claimed that the lesser-known Sullivan had "totally disappeared." The president referred to him as a " fake Alaska candidate ."

Wrote Trump: "Maybe he has been 'kidnapped' by the corrupt Dumocrat lawyers??? They are scared stiff of being prosecuted for election fraud."

An Alaska-based federal judge last month rejected the Justice Department's request to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if the incumbent senator loses. The president has also suggested Peltola should be prosecuted, and Alaska state officials are investigating .

Campaign finance reports show Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has raised and spent relatively little money compared to both the incumbent and Peltola.

09:56 AM ET, November 3 2026, Melissa Montoya

Scenes of democracy unfold as Americans cast ballots on Election Day

Trump says US will cut off aid to Israel by end of the year

09:53 AM ET, November 3 2026, Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy

President Donald Trump said the U.S. will end about $4 billion in annual aid to Israel by the end of the year, saying he had reached an agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Israel's our number one (recipient); we give them more than anybody else. And they no longer need it," said Trump during an interview on Nov. 3 with Fox and Friends. "We've been doing it for years. Israel is a very thriving country. They don't need it."

Trump, speaking on Election Day, said Israel had been a "great ally, much more reliable than most."

U.S. aid to Israel amid the war in Gaza has been one of the most contentious issues leading up to the midterm elections.

Trump also mentioned Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has been an outspoken critic of U.S. military aid to Israel and other countries, arguing that taxpayer dollars should be used to prioritize domestic needs like healthcare and education.

"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like in El Sayed when they don't need it?" said Trump. "It's a bad talking point."

Why are there no NBA games on Election Day?

09:28 AM ET, November 3 2026, Lorenzo Reyes

In a push to get more people out to the ballot box, for the fourth time in five years, the entire NBA will go dark.

The league did not schedule any games Tuesday. Because the first slate of polls closes on the East Coast at 6 p.m. ET, with many more at 7 p.m. ET, holding games would severely interfere with the ability for people who choose to vote in person to do so.

It's one of the three days that the NBA typically avoids scheduling games, joining Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. Read more .

ME Senate race might not be decided tonight

09:01 AM ET, November 3 2026, Margie Cullen

It's "highly possible" that the crucial Maine U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson might not be decided tonight, according to Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.

That's because of Maine's ranked choice voting system .

Maine is one of just two states that uses ranked-choice voting in statewide races with more than two candidates. This year, there are six declared write-in candidates in addition to Jackson and Collins. In ranked choice voting, if no candidate receives over 50% of the first-choice vote, the race goes to a ranked choice tabulation.

"It would be the first time in Maine that a U.S. Senate race has ever gone to ranked choice," Bellows told USA TODAY on Oct. 30. "However, Congressional District Two has gone to ranked choice voting multiple times, so it's highly possible given the tight polling between Collins and Jackson and the existence of the six write-in candidates."

Bellows said ranked choice tabulation has typically taken them until the Friday of the following week after the election to get the official result. This year, that would be Friday, Nov. 13. However, they're hoping to expedite that process if it happens this election.

Scanning machines down in Westchester, New York

08:45 AM ET, November 3 2026, Erin Mansfield

Machines that scan paper ballots are down across Westchester County, New York, a key part of the New York's 17th Congressional District, one of the most competitive races in the country.

Claire Lovell, a poll worker in North Castle, said that the problem started as soon as the polls opened at 6 a.m. and were ongoing after 8 a.m. when she spoke to USA TODAY. She said she was instructed to have voters put their ballots in a secure envelope so they can be hand-counted if the machines don't work.

Elizabeth Belanger, 54, of Sleepy Hollow, said the poll workers in her town told her to either come back later or put the ballot in an envelope. "I decided to go ahead and put in my vote because I was nervous about not having time or not being able to come back later," Belanger said.

Kathleen McGrath, the spokesperson for the New York State Board of Elections, said in a statement that her office is in "constant contact" with the Westchester County Board of Elections. She also reassured voters that their vote is secure.

"Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted," McGrath said. "While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances."

Schumer says Democrats will fight Trump 'tooth and nail' if he doesn't change course

08:41 AM ET, November 3 2026, Bart Jansen

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Democrats could work with Trump if they regain control of the Senate, but only if the president changes his ways and listens to voter concerns about the high cost of living.

"Look, it'll be up to him. Trump has refused to listen to them," Schumer told reporters after voting at a Brooklyn school. "Will he change? I don't know. But we're going to fight Trump tooth and nail, and focus on the issues no matter what he does."

"We'll see if he'll actually change his ways and join," Schumer added. But whether he does or not – because I don't think he will – we are going to keep fighting for the people."

Schumer said Democrats would announce their legislative priorities "soon."

Schumer 'nauseously optimistic' about Democrats regaining control of Senate

08:37 AM ET, November 3 2026, Bart Jansen

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said after voting in New York that Democrats would regain control of the Senate because of their campaign fighting high "costs, chaos and corruption" of the Trump administration.

"We don't want to count our chickens before they hatch so I characterize our mood as nauseously optimistic," Schumer said after voting at Public School 321 in Brooklyn and contributing $10 to a children's bake sale.

He was referring to Democratic nervousness about polling that has sometimes disappointed them in the past. Schumer credited the optimism to Democratic candidates doing well in competitive states and states held by Republicans.

"A year ago nobody thought we could do this," Schumer said. "We recruited good candidates in states people didn't think were winnable."

08:20 AM ET, November 3 2026, Rachel Barber

Americans will cast their ballots based on where politicians stand on a variety of issues, but in poll after poll , their concerns about the cost of living are top of mind.

Inflation remains stubbornly high and above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Consumer prices were up 3.7% over the year in September, outpacing workers' pay growth.

Job growth has slowed over the last two years, but the national unemployment rate hasn't changed much. It was 4.1% in September 2024 and 4.2% in September this year .

By two popular measures, Americans are feeling worse about the economy than they were when they voted in the last presidential election.

The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index dropped to 48 in October, down 31.9% from 70.5 in October 2024. And while the Conference Board's consumer confidence index rose to 91.7 last month, it remains below its revised October 2024 reading of 109.6.

Local and state election officials say they are ready for federal involvement

07:51 AM ET, November 3 2026, Sarah D. Wire

Alarmed by President Donald Trump 's threats of federal involvement, local and state election officials across the United States told USA TODAY they have spent months preparing in case federal officials arrive to enforce immigration laws or seize ballots and voting machines.

They said they have local judges and state attorneys general on speed dial and have briefed governors on how to respond.

Federal officials haven't explicitly said they plan to send federal officers, including immigration officials, to polling places. But they have repeatedly declined to rule out the possibility. Election officials say that means they have an obligation to prepare, just in case.

Seeing extra election monitors at the polls?

07:39 AM ET, November 3 2026, Sarah D. Wire

Dozens of nonpartisan and partisan groups organized tens of thousands of grassroots activists to monitor the polls before and on Election Day . They are prepared in case the Trump administration dispatches immigration officers or other federal officials to election sites.

The effort comes as President Donald Trump and his administration are threatening state and local election officials with criminal charges if noncitizens vote. Meanwhile, federal immigration officers are carrying out mass arrests that have swept up U.S. citizens.

The monitoring will include the period after the election. Community-level organizers have plans for how they will respond this week, if local, state or federal officials challenge election results. In some places, that could mean protesting in the streets, presenters said, or holding news conferences to defend local counts and election officials.

"We have faith in the people who are part of our communities and spend all year preparing to run effective elections. So, we want to have their backs. We want to be able to say, 'No, they were following the law,'" said Andrew Walchuk, policy director and counsel for Common Cause.

Will there be challenges to the election? It depends on how close the outcome is, experts say

07:22 AM ET, November 3 2026, Sarah D. Wire

Multiple election law experts told USA TODAY they are watching for two things on Election Day and the days after: federal presence at the polls and legal attacks based on voter rolls.

The Trump administration has not ruled out the possibility that ICE officers or other federal officials might make an appearance at polling sites. After more than a year of trying unsuccessfully to force states to hand over voter rolls, the administration has already tried to get judges to force county clerks to set aside ballots by people the federal government says might be on the voter rolls despite being ineligible to vote. So far, judges have dismissed these efforts.

Election law experts say they expect legal challenges in contests too close to call on election night, with lawsuits likely to focus on election machines, mail-in ballots and whether noncitizens voted. Those challenges are most likely in races that could determine control of the House or Senate, said Rick Hasen, an elections law expert at the University of California, Los Angeles.

"The margin is the biggest factor," he said. "Some of the polls say that Democrats are going to clean up. If they do, then I don't think any of this stuff's going to make a big difference, but if they don't, if it's very close, then I think you'll see lawsuits all over."

Justice Department sends election monitors to counties and cities in 50 states

07:21 AM ET, November 3 2026, Bart Jansen

The Justice Department released the list of cities and counties where it will send 1,000 election monitors on Nov. 3.

The department called it the "largest monitoring effort in history" in all 50 states.

"Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division said in a statement.

Among the states with the most competitive Senate races, the observers will be in:

Alaska: Anchorage, Dillingham and Kusilvak

Georgia: Cobb, DeKalb, Fulton, Gwinnett, Chatham and Bibb counties

Kansas: Johnson, Wyandotte and Sedgwick counties

Maine: Lewiston, Portland and South Portland

Michigan: Lansing, East Lansing, Grand Rapids, Flint, Detroit, Hamtramck, Warren and Dearborn

Ohio: Cuyahoga, Franklin and Medina counties.

Texas: Bexar, Dallas, Harris, Waller, Blanco, Bowie and Nueces counties

Trump blasts challengers to Republicans in Senate races in Alaska, Michigan

07:04 AM ET, November 3 2026, Bart Jansen

Trump continued his criticism of candidates in overnight social media posts about two competitive Senate races.

In Alaska, Trump said independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan is "MISSING IN ACTION!" in the campaign against incumbent GOP Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election if the challenger gets enough votes to cost the incumbent the race with Democrat Mary Peltola. But the judge dismissed the case on Sunday. Polls call the race a toss-up .

In Michigan, Trump continued disparaging Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers. Trump said "Only fools would vote for" El-Sayed and he encouraged people to "VOTE FOR MIKE ROGERS."

Recent polling showed El-Sayed leading Rogers. But the surveys were conducted before Democrat Haley Stevens, who was beaten by El-Sayed in the primary, crossed party lines Sunday to endorse Rogers.

Former Trump ally predicts 'referendum' on Trump

06:45 AM ET, November 3 2026, Michael Loria

Former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene , R-Georgia, said Monday evening that she expects the midterms to be a referendum on President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress who supported his agenda.

"It's a complete referendum on Donald Trump, his betrayal, where he promised no more foreign wars and to bring world peace, " Greene told CNN, listing some of the president's worst offenses in her estimation. "And also not listening to everyday Americans who are saying we cannot afford the cost of living, we cannot afford health insurance, we cannot afford these high prices of gas and diesel, while he is constantly bragging about a ballroom and his big donors and having these big fancy dinners, as if he can't even relate to the American people."

Greene, a former Trump ally, broke with the president in November 2025 over the president's apparent hesitation or unwillingness to pursue justice for the victims of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein .

She also slammed Republicans in Congress who continue supporting Trump, warning voters won't welcome their loyalty to the president.

"They just stood behind him, applauding everything he said, every lie he told, and never fought back for the American people who gave them the majority," she said.

Ahead of midterms, Trump defends Iran war

06:26 AM ET, November 3 2026, Michael Loria

President Donald Trump defended the U.S. war on Iran in an interview on Fox News Monday evening, just hours before polls open.

"We cannot let them have a nuclear weapon and we won't," Trump told Fox News anchor Sean Hannity, justifying the war he and U.S. ally Israel launched on Feb. 28.

The war has seen long stretches without fighting but has become deeply unpopular , in part because it has driven fuel prices to their highest levels in years. Other concerns include its rising $47.1 billion price tag, reports of sinking morale among troops, and the deaths of at least 21 U.S. service members.

Trump on Monday night batted away criticisms, arguing that it's not a war, though he hinted that the United States could attack Iran again if they don't make a deal to end the conflict.

"There's no war raging. It could happen if they don't make a deal. But they want to make a deal very badly," said Trump, repeating claims about the intentions of Iran's leaders that Tehran has derided as largely false throughout the war.

Iran war death toll grows. See the list of US service members killed

Two American soldiers were killed in an attack in Jordan, including Isabella Gonzalez, raising the U.S. military death toll in the Iran war to 17. Pvt. Gonzales, killed in action in an Iranian attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in this image taken at a location given as Germany, released on July 20, 2026.

articles.title: Final midterm projections give Democrats high odds to sweep Congress
articles.summary: Forecasters and prediction markets give Democrats strong odds to sweep Congress, but past polling misses loom.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The polls on the East Coast are open, and with that comes the end of prediction season. Democrats are hoping they aren't being set up for another polling let-down.

Forecasting models and prediction markets have gone from guardedly optimistic to more confident that the Democrats will take the Senate as well as the House. Decision Desk HQ, which partners with NewsNation for race calls, gives them a 63% chance to control the House and Senate in 2027. They give Republicans a 15% chance to do the same.

DDHQ is more confident in the Democrats' chances of winning the House, which they predict will go blue to the tune of around 241 seats.

Republicans were projected to win the Senate as recently as Labor Day weekend, but the Democrats' odds in DDHQ's estimation have shot up in the last couple of months. They project the Democrats will win 52 seats — one more than they would need.

Prediction markets are even more bullish. Polymarket has the Democrats at a 75% chance to sweep, while Kalshi is a tick below that at 74%. Silver Bulletin , run by election modeler Nate Silver, puts Democrats' odds of a sweep at 82%.

A recent New York Times-Sienna poll paints a picture of a big night for Democrats, but we've seen this before, only for Democrats to underperform relative to those expectations. Presidential elections in 2016, 2020 and 2024 each saw Republican candidates underrepresented in polls by around 3-5%, according to Silver Bulletin. If you apply that error to many races in this election, the Democrats likely don't take the Senate and the House may be closer than everyone is expecting.

NewsNation provides comprehensive coverage of the 2026 midterm elections like never before, with live results powered by Decision Desk HQ and expert analysis. Stay tuned for race calls after the polls close Tuesday night.

But the story in midterm polls hasn't been as dramatic. In 2018 and 2022, the polling error in favor of Democrats was less than 1%, per Silver Bulletin.

Midterm elections 'toss up' races to watch

DDHQ lists eight Senate seats in "lean" or "toss up" categories: Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Alaska, South Carolina, Texas, Maine and Nebraska. At the beginning of the year, Democratic wins in at least six of those states were borderline unthinkable. Maine has always represented hope for Democrats because it tends to vote blue, despite electing Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, time after time.

Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate in Ohio, is nearly two years removed from serving in the Senate, so it would be less surprising to see him return than to see Kansas send its first Democratic senator to Washington since the 1930s.

Stick with NewsNation as results come in tonight. We will have special election coverage Tuesday night starting at 7p/6C with Chris Cuomo, Elizabeth Vargas, Leland Vittert, Katie Pavlich and Chris Stirewalt.

articles.title: Paxton, Talarico battle for Texas Senate seat: Election Day live updates
articles.summary: Texans head to the polls Tuesday to decide key races, including the U.S. Senate contest between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
articles.body:
Texans head to the polls today to cast decisive votes in races that will shape the nation's and the state's future.

Chief among them is the nationally watched and debated U.S. Senate race in Texas , where Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarcio are seeking to replace U.S. Sen. John Cornyn.

On a state level, Gov. Greg Abbott is seeing the tightest reelection campaign since being elected to office in 2014. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa is seeking to replace him as the first Democrat elected to office in over 30 years and the first Latina in state history.

Follow along throughout the day as we bring you live coverage of what is happening in Texas throughout Election Day.

Inside President Donald Trump's red state midterm blitz — Photos

What are the odds in the Texas governor's race?

11:01 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

Here's a look at the two biggest prediction markets as of 8 a.m. on Nov. 3 and what they say about the Texas governor's race.

Who will win the Texas governor's race between Greg Abbott, Gina Hinojosa?

Polymarket: Abbott 64%, Hinojosa 37%. Market volume = $3,075,821.

Kalshi: Abbott 65%, Hinojosa 35%. Market volume = $19,191,934.

Who will win the Texas Senate and governor's races (combo)?

Combo markets price specific split-ticket outcomes, letting traders bet on both races together.

Greg Abbott and James Talarico win — 42%

Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico win — 35%

Greg Abbott and James Talarico win — 44%

Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico win — 33%

10:24 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

For the first time in more than three decades, a Texas Democrat is heading into November within striking distance of the governor's mansion — and she would make history if she wins.

Hinojosa, a five-term Austin lawmaker, is polling within the margin of error against Abbott — a three-term incumbent who has never won reelection by fewer than 11 points in the past few months.

A final poll from the New York Times/Siena University , released Nov. 1, shows Hinojosa and Abbott are statistically tied, 48% to 47%.

U of H Hobby poll (Oct. 18) — Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 46%.

Marist poll (Oct. 14) — Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 45%.

UT/Texas Politics Project (Oct. 13) — Hinojosa 49%, Abbott 48%

ReconMR (Oct. 13) — Abbott 48%, Hinojosa 47%

UMass Lowell (Oct. 8) — Abbott 48%, Hinojosa 44%.

YouGov poll (Oct. 6 ) — Hinojosa 48%, Abbott 47%.

The New York Times (Oct. 3) — Hinojosa 49%, Abbott 46%.

Fox News (Oct. 1) — Abbott 52%, Hinojosa 47%.

10:18 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

Here's a look at the two biggest prediction markets as of 8 a.m. on Nov. 3 and what they are saying about the Texas Senate race.

Who will win the Texas U.S. Senate race between Ken Paxton, James Talarico?

Polymarket: Talarico 74%, Paxton 26%. Market volume = $13,567,779.

Kalshi: Talarico 73%, Paxton 27%. Market volume = $89,636,005.

Here is a look at the top four margins traders are trading on.

Texas congressional races to watch tonight

10:00 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

Three congressional races in Texas are giving the Republican Party a headache, as political analysis shows they are shifting toward Democrats.

These three races are among 15 U.S. House races nationwide whose ratings have shifted, suggesting Republicans are on track to lose the House majority in the midterm elections, according to The Cook Political Report .

Texas' 35th District — Democrat Johnny Garcia vs. Republican Carlos De La Cruz

Texas' 9th District — Republican Alex Mealer vs. Democrat Leticia Gutierrez.

The last race is between Democrat Bobby Pulido , the Tejano singer-songwriter, and incumbent Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas' 15th Congressional District.

Texas early voting: How 2026 compares with 2022 and 2024

09:45 AM ET, November 3 2026, Brandi D. Addison

More than 7.7 million Texans voted early ahead of the 2026 midterms, according to figures through Oct. 30.

That's about 1.3 million fewer early votes than ahead of the 2024 presidential election, but about 2.2 million more than ahead of the 2022 gubernatorial election.

Election Day voting totals will provide a fuller picture of participation in this year's midterms.

Recent Talarico-Paxton Texas Senate polls

09:45 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

Since Ken Paxton won the Republican primary runoff in May, polls have shown him and James Talarico statistically tied within the margin of error.

The gap between the two didn't start to grow until early fall, when Talarico led outside the margin of error.

A final poll from the New York Times /Siena College , released Nov. 1, shows Talarico leading Paxton , 50% to 43% — a 7-point lead outside the poll's margin.

Texas early voting surpasses 7.7 million ahead of Election Day

09:01 AM ET, November 3 2026, Brandi D. Addison

More than 7.7 million Texans had cast ballots before Election Day, according to statewide turnout figures from the secretary of state office.

About 7.5 million voted early in person, while roughly 281,000 cast mail ballots.

That's fewer than the 9.1 million early votes recorded ahead of the 2024 presidential election, but more than the 5.5 million cast ahead of the 2022 midterms.

09:01 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

While polls have been open for an hour across most of Texas, voting is just getting underway in El Paso and Hudspeth counties.

The two counties are in the Mountain Time Zone, while most of Texas is in the Central Time Zone. Polls close at 7 p.m. local time statewide.

Harris County tops Texas in early ballots cast

08:26 AM ET, November 3 2026, Brandi D. Addison

Harris County reported the most early ballots in Texas through Oct. 30, with about 1.07 million.

Dallas County ranked second with 624,000, followed by Tarrant County with 587,000, Bexar County with 526,000 and Travis County with 444,000.

Together, the five counties accounted for about 3.3 million early ballots.

08:01 AM ET, November 3 2026, Mateo Rosiles

It is Election Day in Texas, and the nation's eyes are on the state as it waits to see whether Democratic hopeful James Talarico can flip one of the state's U.S. Senate seats blue against Republican candidate Ken Paxton.

Texans are also watching to see whether any statewide offices will flip blue this cycle—most notably the governor's seat, as Gov. Greg Abbott is running for his fourth term.

He faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the contest — who, if she wins, would be the first Latina governor in the state's history and the first Democrat to hold the governor's seat in over 30 years.

articles.title: Rising cost of living tops voters’ concerns as midterm ballots cast
articles.summary: The rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with President Trump are the top concerns for nearly half of voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, a...
articles.body:
The rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with President Trump are the top concerns for nearly half of voters heading into Tuesday's midterm elections , according to a new survey.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll , released late Monday, found that 48 percent of registered voters ranked the cost of living as the most important factor in deciding their vote, far outpacing concerns about democracy, at 26 percent, and immigration, at 13 percent.

The findings highlight the economic frustrations facing Republicans as they fight to maintain control of Congress amid difficult political terrain. Many Americans reported that their household finances have deteriorated since Trump returned to the White House.

Nearly half of Americans, 49 percent, said their financial situation has worsened during Trump's second term, compared with just 13 percent who said it has improved. Another 37 percent reported little change, the data shows.

The economic pessimism was particularly strong among Hispanic respondents, with 54 percent saying their finances had worsened under the Trump administration, while just 10 percent reported an improvement.

Americans have also grappled with higher fuel prices tied to the unpopular U.S.-Israeli war with Iran — which entered its eighth month heading into the elections, adding to broader concerns about affordability.

The national average price for a gallon of gas sits at $4.15 as of Tuesday morning, according to AAA , up more than a dollar from a year ago.

The Iran conflict itself has also become a political liability for the president. Just 25 percent of voters said the military operations against Iran have been worth their costs, compared with 55 percent who said they have not. Another 18 percent were unsure, the survey found.

The cost of the U.S.'s war against Iran has risen to $47 billion — up $3 billion from September — with the biggest chunk of the cost going to munition replacement.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online among 1,765 U.S. adults ahead of Election Day. It has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: When will we know midterm election results? Details on the process
articles.summary: It is Election Day, but it doesn't mean results will come out today. Here's what to know as votes are being tabulated across the country.
articles.body:
It's Election Day , but the wait for results and winners of pivotal races across the country could go deep into the night and into the week, which, contrary to what various politicians have snarked at, is completely normal.

In the lead-up to the midterm elections and in previous years, President Donald Trump has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that widespread fraud exists in mail-in voting. He has also raised suspicion of the speed of vote counting in certain states.

But in an interview with Politifact, Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert, says counting speed depends on states' own rules and laws.

"States are neither fast nor slow; they all count and certify the results in accordance with the laws passed by their state legislature," Macias said. "What is fast or slow is how quickly the media can collect sufficient evidence to confidently predict the winner, which is typically based on the margin of victory."

Here is what you need to know about when midterm election results could come in.

‘I voted’ stickers show unique election pride at midterm polls

According to Reuters , the first calls will start soon after polls begin to close. Indiana and Kentucky will close first at 6 p.m. ET, and Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, and Virginia will close at 7 p.m. ET. In some races, an instant call may occur if much of the voting has already taken place.

Most news outlets' calls will rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press or election-data firm Decision Desk HQ.

Per Reuters, outlets like the Wall Street Journal and ‌MS NOW will rely on the AP for race calls, while others like Fox News and CBS News will make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling.

Mail-in ballots could make the wait longer

According to the Center for Election Innovation & Research , 13 of 50 states allow mail-in ballots to be received and counted after Election Day as long as they were postmarked on or before Election Day, with some, like Washington state, having a deadline as late as Nov. 23.

Here are the states that allow for these later mail-in ballots, including the latest day they can be received:

Beyond the various deadlines for mail-in ballots across the country, rules also vary on when states can begin processing and counting absentee and mail-in ballots.

According to the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) , 17 states and the U.S. Virgin Islands prohibit scanning absentee ballots until Election Day, which can delay the counting process. Of these, seven states permit scanning only after the polls close: Alabama, Alaska, Idaho, Illinois, Mississippi, New Hampshire and West Virginia.

How long it takes absentee/mail-in ballots to be counted and extended deadlines have led to a phenomenon commonly known as the "blue shift" and "red mirage," which have changed how people see results come in, sometimes having one candidate leading during the night to then be behind by the time people wake up.

Both became subjects of discussion during the 2020 election , when Election Day ballots were counted first because they were cast in person, while mail-in/absentee ballots were counted hours and days after.

Historically, Election Day voters have skewed more Republican, while Democrats have skewed more toward casting absentee/mail-in ballots.

That split can cause a Republican candidate to lead early in the night as Election Day ballots are counted, known as the "red mirage," before the gap narrows or even reverses as absentee and mail-in ballots are tabulated in a "blue shift."

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.
