articles.title: The unlikely player in contentious Michigan Senate race: Stevens's fiancé
articles.summary: Months before the high-stakes Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, Jason Turkish took such a hands-on role in Rep. Haley Stevens's campaign that her senior...
articles.body:
Months before the high-stakes Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, Jason Turkish took such a hands-on role in Rep. Haley Stevens's campaign that her senior staff called a meeting without her to devise how to restrict his role, according to multiple people familiar with the meeting.

Turkish was seen as relatively new to Stevens's orbit. Most of the congresswoman's senior staff knew him as a top donor some had met earlier in the campaign, which launched in 2025.

By early June, Stevens and Turkish were said to be secretly engaged, according to multiple former campaign staffers who said the one-time donor had become Stevens's most important adviser. Stevens soon added him to private campaign text chains, one of the reasons staff called a meeting to figure out how to curtail his interactions with the team, according to one of the people familiar with the meeting.

Tensions between staffers and a candidate's spouse or significant other are not uncommon in a campaign's intense atmosphere. They tend to erupt in crisis moments, and Stevens was facing tough polling in her race with Abdul El-Sayed.

Now questions about Turkish's role in Stevens's primary campaign have been revived in the general election's closing hours, after the Democratic congresswoman's 11th-hour reversal of support for El-Sayed, the progressive Democrat who won the primary. This account is based on interviews with more than a dozen former Stevens campaign aides and other people familiar with the campaign.

Stevens, 43, said that "any campaign staff being directly quoted in this article, I was made miserable by working with them."

Asked whether she felt her campaign staff was trying to push out Turkish or limit his influence in any way, Stevens said, "I have nothing else to say about the campaign at this time."

Turkish, a 39-year-old disability lawyer and political fundraiser, would not comment on whether staff sought to curtail his role, but he provided to The Washington Post emails from June and July showing that staff continued to reach out and consult him on campaign matters. He declined to address specific claims by former campaign staff on the record.

"I was Haley Stevens's energetic and passionate supporter from the very launch of this campaign," he said. "And while the campaign ended in defeat, it also ended in our marriage. And along the path of that campaign, we spent thousands of hours together and around a campaign. And there were good days and bad days, but we lived it together, and we wouldn't trade it for anything."

Turkish lives in Huntington Woods, a suburb north of Detroit, and works in Southfield as a managing partner at Nyman Turkish, a litigation and disability law firm. The Detroit News reported that the two met after Stevens's 2022 reelection campaign through David Kramer, a mutual friend.

Stevens initially backed El-Sayed after their bruising primary, even telling people he was a "great candidate," but over the course of the general election, her public support for the candidate grew more strained, particularly as it related to El-Sayed's stance on Israel's war with Hamas, where he has become a leading voice denouncing U.S. support in what he labels a "genocide."

Turkish endorsed El-Sayed's opponent in the key Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers, days before Stevens shocked the political world by backing Rogers and appearing with him at church on Sunday with Turkish. In an interview revealing his choice, he told the Detroit News that he saw an "escalation" in the Democratic nominee's rhetoric around Israel.

Stevens's endorsement has led some close to her to express concern about Turkish's influence on her decision, including longtime friends, one who spoke with her as recently as Saturday night, mere hours before she backed Rogers on Sunday. The endorsement has effectively led Stevens to be excommunicated from her state's party, with the head of the Michigan Democratic Party writing that she was "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Stevens said "any suppositions that Jason Turkish influenced me on Israel or campaign positions is absurd."

Late Monday night, Stevens posted a lengthy explanation for her decision on X that lamented how "some critics have also dragged my fiancé into this, suggesting he or others must have made my decision for me."

"Think about what that says. A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings," she wrote. "That is sexism dressed up as political analysis."

One friend who spoke with Stevens said the congresswoman reassured her Saturday night that she would "never" rescind her endorsement of El-Sayed.

"That primary was particularly brutal. For all involved," the friend said. "I feel that there is like an allegiance to him because he was there for her during a particularly dark and stressful time."

But one aide said Stevens trusted Turkish and often valued his insight, particularly on Israel, because she agreed with him more than with her advisers, who were pushing her to be less supportive of Israel. After her endorsement of Rogers, many Israel supporters have applauded both Stevens and Turkish for what they view as a tough, gutsy stance.

"By the time I got to the place where I was ready to do it, I would have been living a lie to a lot of people and in community. ... There was no way to circle the square," Stevens told the Detroit News on Monday.

Stevens's senior staff first grew troubled by Turkish's campaign influence around June, people familiar with the campaign said.

According to multiple people familiar with the exchanges, Turkish started berating staff for their work, particularly perplexed that he, a Stevens supporter, was being served digital ads about the campaign. He wanted more spent on digital fundraising, and he summoned a senior digital campaign staffer to his law office and yelled at her over the kind of digital content and fundraising emails the campaign was creating, the people said. He told a press aide that she was "not serving Haley well," two people familiar with the conversation recalled.

Turkish would also send the congresswoman a list of hurtful tweets people were writing about her, four people familiar with Turkish's influence on Stevens said. Campaign staff also worried that when Turkish was the last person to speak with Stevens before an interview or event, she would stray from the campaign's talking points, the people said.

"He was not a calming presence, in a way that in hindsight should have been more alarming," said Caitlin Legacki, a former top adviser to Stevens's campaign. "It was very strange. I have never seen anything like it."

One former Stevens aide said campaign staff worked to prevent Turkish from showing up to events because of how he undermined staff. If he arrived, the person said, they would redirect cameras or reposition Stevens so that he could not draw the attention of the press. Before events, they said he often suggested rewriting talking points and insisted on joining Stevens's briefings before media appearances.

The team tried to control his influence with two guardrails, multiple people said: Making sure he was not the last person to speak with Stevens before a public-facing event, and outlining how he was only allowed to go directly through the campaign's manager, Sam Barrett, not directly to lower-level staff, according to multiple sources familiar with the guardrails.

"It did not work in the sense that he had any less influence on Haley," said Legacki, who left the campaign after it became public she was also working for the tech company Palantir while advising the campaign.

Stevens said in an interview for this article that Legacki "was fired" because "of undisclosed conflicts."

The changes meant Stevens's schedule was sometimes altered to ensure she spoke with a campaign staffer, and no one else, before certain events or calls, the people said.

"We would organize the schedule to make sure there was a staff member who would be the last person talking to her because she did an interview or a donor call," said a person familiar with the campaign.

Longtime friends say the couple grew even closer after her defeat.

The morning after Stevens's primary loss to El-Sayed - a closer result than the polls anticipated - former Michigan governor James Blanchard (D) called her, thinking she would need some consoling, he said. Instead, she sounded ebullient.

"I'm getting married!" she told Blanchard.

articles.title: US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as the Mideast ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle Ea...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.

The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.

Trump said Israel doesn't need the aid and it's a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel .

Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship.

"You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash," Trump said. "Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money."

There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office. But at least some of his political opponents were cautious.

Yair Golan, a leader in Israel's opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a "severe blow to Israel's security" at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts. "The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public," Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement.

Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel

The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years.

In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel's ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.

Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.

He told The Economist in January that he wanted to "taper off" U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was "in the works."

Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment

But the optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.

"The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it's no secret — as a signal of unfairness," Trump said Tuesday on Fox. "And we can't allow that to happen. I don't like that, because it's too easy. It's almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we've agreed. He was very understanding of it."

Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years.

There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.

In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.

Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.

There was more aid after the Gaza war started

An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict .

Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years.

While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East.

articles.title: What do I need to bring to vote in Virginia? Election Day guide
articles.summary: If you're heading to vote on Election Day in Virginia, the state has a list of items you are allowed or not allowed to bring with you.
articles.body:
Polls are open in Virginia, but there are a few things eligible voters must know before they visit their polling place.

Virginia has specific rules about voter identification and what people can bring inside polling places.

Here's a look at what voters should know before casting their ballots.

What do Virginia voters need to bring to their polling place?

Virginia voters should bring an acceptable form of identification when they visit their polling place.

Voters do not need to bring proof of their voter registration, but they must either show an acceptable ID or sign an ID confirmation statement before casting a regular ballot.

Do I need to bring an ID to vote in Virginia?

Yes, Virginia requires voters to provide an acceptable form of identification when voting in person, although the ID does not have to include a photograph.

Acceptable forms of ID include: Virginia driver's license (even an expired license), valid U.S. passport or passport card, valid military identification, valid student identification issued by a Virginia high school or university, Virginia voter identification card, government-issued identification documents or a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other qualifying government document containing the voter's name and address.

What can I bring to my Virginia polling place?

You can bring children under 15 with you to vote as long as they do not disrupt or interfere with normal voting procedures.

Virginia law allows voters to take sample ballots into the voting booth, but they cannot give, show or display the sample ballot to another person inside the polling place or within the restricted area outside it, except to an authorized assistant.

Voters are also allowed to wear campaign-related clothing and accessories displaying a candidate's name or political message.

What can't I bring to my Virginia polling place?

Virginia law prohibits knowingly carrying a firearm within 100 feet of a building, or part of a building, being used as a polling place. Certain exceptions apply, including for qualified law enforcement officers and licensed armed security officers performing their duties.

Voters may bring electronic devices, including cellphones, into Virginia polling places, but election officers can limit their use if they disrupt voting, cause delays or interfere with another person's ability to cast a ballot.

articles.title: On Election Day, We All Get to Be Haley Stevens and Pick the (Hopefully) Less Lousy Candidates
articles.summary: Once again, Americans will have to live with the consequences of their political choices.
articles.body:
However they voted, Americans waking up Wednesday morning can probably sympathize with Rep. Haley Stevens (D–Mich.), who surprised campaign watchers by rescinding her support for her party's Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, and endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the race. After her past harsh words for the GOP hopeful, Stevens seems an unlikely Rogers fan. Instead, it appears she concluded that he sucks less than the Democrat and cast her lot accordingly. Most voters can sympathize.

In the past, Stevens called out Rogers as a " MAGA grifter " and " an out-of-touch, out-of-state millionaire ." That's pointed, but it's standard-issue political rhetoric for 2026. Those taunts pale in comparison to the charge, leveled in her video announcing the about-face , of "hate… from our Democratic nominee." Stevens also criticized El-Sayed's association with Hasan Piker, the communist-curious influencer who frequently lashes out at Israel and Jews .

Stevens, whose pro-Israel stance is well-known, broke with El-Sayed after he refused to denounce an antisemitic ad targeted at Rogers that had been produced by a PAC associated with Piker's uncle, media personality Cenk Uygur. Earlier this year, El-Sayed also infamously shrugged off a terrorist attack on a Michigan synagogue by saying "hurt people hurt people."

It's easy to see how Stevens could conclude that a grifter is less odious than El-Sayed's inclinations.

Americans seem to make similar calculations as their political choices swing wildly between America's two entrenched major parties, through the ideological mutations suffered by those organizations.

Americans Habitually Pick What They Hope is the Less Awful Option

In May, Pew Research reported that "58% of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of the Republican Party" while "a nearly identical share (59%) have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party." Twenty-six percent can't stand either one.

That's not to say the Democratic and Republican parties no longer have enthusiastic partisans—they certainly do. True believers loyally cast primary ballots to select party standard-bearers who seem increasingly capable of ginning up excitement among a small segment of the population while repelling normies. In 1988, the earliest year surveyed by Gallup , voters roughly divided themselves in thirds among Democrats, independents, and Republicans. The two parties now each claim the support of just over a quarter of the electorate while independents represent 45 percent of voters.

Ultimately, those independents generally fall into line to vote for Republicans or Democrats, but they do so as less-bad alternatives to what they really dislike.

"Majorities of Republican leaners (56%) and Democratic leaners (64%) say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is that the other party's policies are harmful," Pew noted last month. "Relatively few Republican leaners (34%) and Democratic leaners (27%) say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is the perceived good of its policies."

The Trick Is Selling the Other Guy as Worse

We've created a political system in which everybody gets to be Haley Stevens for a day—or much longer, really, given the now never-ending nature of campaigning. We all pick the (we hope) less bad option.

The trick, of course, is deciding which candidate or party is awful rather than evil, and therefore less undeserving of a vote and election to political office. That's why so little of our political discourse delves into the relative merits of competing policy proposals and so much involves warnings about the inevitable doom to befall us if those people win. We hear very little "candidate X is great" and a lot of "candidate X is a corrupt pedo who will raise prices and end the republic."

That's pretty much the tone of the political ads in the piece of Arizona where I live.

What's remarkable is that there's little evidence that political advertising works. A 2020 Yale study found that "ads' effect on whom individuals intended to vote for was…a statistically insignificant 0.007 of a percentage point." That said, 2021 research from Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management found some impact from political advertising, but that "negative ones were more effective at swaying voters' decisions."

Advertising also boosts name recognition. So, if you're going to do it at all, it makes sense to go with the odds and the tone of the moment and embrace the dark side.

That doesn't mean voters all come to the same conclusion about which party or candidates are more repulsive. Based on their values and priorities, and the degree to which they're angry about the state of the world around them, Americans make very different decisions about who sucks less. They argue about those conclusions with friends, neighbors, and strangers who make contrary choices about who to vote against, with participants absolutely convinced that this time they've identified the real danger.

Buyer's Remorse Is the Inevitable Outcome

Often, these debates take place among people who came to different conclusions about who was the bigger threat in the last election cycle, and the one before that. Voters then typically suffer buyer's remorse over the conduct of politicians who emerged victorious from the last round of balloting.

"Since 1946, there have been 20 midterm elections," Robert A. Strong, a senior fellow at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, wrote in January. "In 18 of them, the president's party lost seats in the House of Representatives. That's 90% of the midterm elections in the past 80 years."

In September, a survey by Navigator Research "found 18 percent of 2024 Trump voters regretted their vote." That's pretty close to the 20 percent of voters who cast their votes for Joe Biden in 2020 that told Zogby pollsters the next year they regretted how they filled out their ballots.

In a world where many people cast votes against the candidates they think are worse, it's unsurprising that dissatisfaction with the victors is a regular feature of the political process.

It's fair to ask, at this point, who I'm voting against. Well, after years of trying to parse the most pressing danger in each election cycle only to see the winners, some of whom I supported, treat the aftermath of the election as a hold-my-beer moment, I decided not to cast a ballot at all.

This year, I experience no buyer's remorse for my political decisions. I only have to suffer the consequences of others' bad choices. Like Haley Stevens, I'm sure they all hope they chose less wrong.

articles.title: Midterms 2026 live updates: Election Day voters head to the polls as Democrats look to flip GOP control of the House and Senate
articles.summary: Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control of Congress as Republicans fight to hold on to their majorities and President Trump looks to help the GOP avert a so-called blue wave.
articles.body: Election Day is here. Today, voters across the United States are heading to the polls to cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms. And with control of Congress up for grabs, the stakes are high for both parties as President Trump heads into his final two years in office.Democrats are seeking to regain control of both the House and Senate, while Republicans, who have held narrow majorities in both chambers since January 2025, are seeking to retain control.In the House, there are 435 seats. And while all of them are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% (or about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. The GOP currently holds 218 seats, compared with 214 held by Democrats. One seat is occupied by an independent (Rep. Kevin Kiley of California), and there are two vacancies (seats formerly held by GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas and Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick of Florida, who each resigned). To retake control of the House, Democrats would need a net gain of four seats. In the Senate, there are 100 seats, with 35 up for grabs and 12-or-so considered competitive. Republicans currently hold 53 seats compared with 45 held by Democrats. There are two independents — Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine — who caucus with the Democrats. To wrest back control of the Senate, Democrats would need a net gain of four seats. To maintain Senate control, Republicans could still lose a net of three seats, since a 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.There are also 36 gubernatorial races and numerous ballot measures to keep an eye on.Trump, whose approval ratings are at or near all-time lows, has spent the last month campaigning in battleground states, urging voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot to encourage higher turnout in hopes that it'll help Republicans avert a so-called blue wave. Some members of the GOP, however, appear to be bracing for one."It could be quite a brutal evening," one senior GOP official told Politico. "Once the dominoes start falling, it becomes hard to stop them."

articles.title: Collins’s Maine office vandalized on eve of election
articles.summary: A federal constituent service office of Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) was vandalized overnight for the second time within the last two months as the incumbent winds down a tight race to hold on to her seat. Photos obtained by NewsNation show red paint was used to write “blood on her hands” and was also splashed…
articles.body:
A federal constituent service office of Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) was vandalized overnight for the second time within the last two months as the incumbent winds down a tight race to hold on to her seat.

Photos obtained by NewsNation show red paint was used to write “blood on her hands” and was also splashed onto the sidewalk outside Collins’s Biddeford office. The town is where Venezuelan migrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by an immigration officer earlier this year.

Collins, speaking with a CBS reporter in Maine, called the incident “disgraceful.”

“Last night we once again had vandalism at my federal office in Biddeford. This office does constituent service work. This is not a political office. It’s always there, helping people with problems with Social Security or Veterans Benefits or the IRS,” she said.

“This is so unacceptable, and it’s unfair to my caseworkers who are working there. And fortunately, they refuse to be intimidated by this. And the office is open and doing business today.”

Collins’s chief of staff, Katie Brown, said in a statement the move was meant to “intimidate the Senator and her staff.”

“These tactics are disturbing, but not effective. Our staff is undeterred and on the job,” she said.

The Biddeford office was also vandalized in September with a reference to President Trump, while Collins has also said her Bangor home was egged that same month.

Collins, the only Republican senator from New England, is running against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.

articles.title: GOP braces for midterms wipeout as Trump rants about Reflecting Pool algae?
articles.summary: Fixing the Reflecting Pool is not a major concern of voters in Michigan or Texas or Alaska. And that’s a problem.
articles.body:
Today, voters have a chance to sound off on whether they endorse the actions of President Trump and the Republican Party throughout his second term in office, or whether they would feel more comfortable handing the reins over to House and Senate Democrats, who will immediately launch investigations of the Trump family, Republican officials and top Republican donors like Elon Musk.

The campaigns are making their closing arguments, and here was what was on Trump’s mind as he made his final pitch to voters that they should stick by him, and not allow far-left Democrats to thwart his agenda.

Look, I am glad that the president has finally gotten that Reflecting Pool algae under control, after a bungled attempt that involved a contractor who screwed it up. As a D.C. resident, I’m glad the fountains are working again, and that the presence of the National Guard is deterring crime. There’s a lot of positive things to say about Trump’s impact on the nation’s capital.

But Trump is not running to be mayor of the district of Columbia. He is president of the United States, and his Republican candidates are facing significant challenges in states where they should be comfortably ahead.

He needs to be laser focused on convincing voters in those states that they have to stick with the GOP, because the alternative is to embolden a rival party on the precipice of succumbing to socialism. He needs to explain that he’s wrapping up the war in Iran and working on those diesel prices. He needs to tout the successes of the administration on eliminating burdensome regulations and making government more efficient by reducing the size of the federal workforce. He can talk about what he’s done to curb illegal immigration, one of the major concerns of voters.

And perhaps most of all, he can remind the American people that the Democratic Party is going to wage war on wealth creation, on housing creation, on new construction, and on your bank account in the form of taxes and regulation. This is a party that is ready to massively expand the federal government by spending way more money on health care and education, which we all know will not actually make these services better.

Fixing the Reflecting Pool is not a major concern of voters in Michigan or Texas or Alaska. And that’s a problem.

Look, it’s too late to undo the costly Iran War, or make the DOGE initiative more successful, or address corruption charges by hiring more competent personnel. But it’s never too late to get the agenda back on track, or to point out the flaws on the other side. I don’t think D.C. park projects is accomplishing that task.

Now. we’ve all seen the polls, which are currently predicting a total GOP wipeout . If polls are accurate, the Republicans will lose control of the House and also the Senate, where they should have had a structural advantage. If Trump beats the polls again, we can finally consign this entire industry to the dustbin of history. But it’s worth noting that prediction markets also have the president’s party badly under-performing. Not a good sign.

It looks like it’s all going to come down to Maine, Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Alaska and possibly Iowa. If the Dems fail to defend their Michigan seat, then they would need to have an extremely good night everywhere else, which does not seem very likely to me. On the other hand, if the GOP loses Texas, a bloodbath is likely to ensue.

So that’s where things stand. The president still has much to accomplish in his second term, and so Americans need to decide if they want to see that happen or if they prefer the paralysis and infighting that is usually characteristic of divided government.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed soars in Kalshi odds after Haley Stevens fallout
articles.summary: Whether this changes votes tonight remains to be seen. But Stevens’s decision has certainly changed the conversation and, unexpectedly, brought Democrats together around Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.body:
The fallout from Congresswoman Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers has been extraordinary, but it has also been a benefit to Abdul El-Sayed.

Prediction markets have continued to price El-Sayed favorably. Kalshi’s market showed him around 78 to 79 percent by Monday morning. Those numbers are not polling, and markets fluctuate, but they certainly don’t suggest Stevens’s endorsement has fundamentally changed the market’s assessment of the race.

Then the money came rolling in. Check out this X post from MSNOW executive producer Kyle Griffin: “According to El-Sayed’s campaign, Sunday brought in more than $2.4 million, its biggest fundraising day yet. More than 65,000 donors contributed, with an average donation of $36.74. Nearly 30,000 were first-time donors.”

That’s some pretty remarkable fundraising response in the middle of a political melodrama. But the way this has backfired and the unorganized rollout of this dramatic decision makes me wonder if Haley Stevens is OK.

The New Republic published a headline reading: “Haley Stevens’s Friends and Staffers Are Freaked Out by Her Fiancé,” detailing concerns allegedly raised by people in her inner circle about Jason Turkish and his influence over the congresswoman.

Michigan University regent Jordan Acker, a friend of Stevens, publicly said he was “deeply troubled” by Turkish’s alleged treatment of Stevens’s staff, friends and allies. Acker also claimed he couldn’t reach Stevens because Turkish had taken her phone. He also wrote: “I’ve heard serious concerns about his treatment of Haley’s staff, friends, and allies. My own experiences have only deepened those concerns.”

We have no idea what’s happening privately in their relationship, but these are uncomfortable allegations, and if Stevens was going to make a decision this consequential, you’d think she’d be prepared to explain it.

Instead, watch this exchange with Anderson Cooper on CNN:

STEVENS: “We all want Democrats to win, I’m a really proud Democrat, and by the way, Abdul has every other Democrat with him.”

COOPER: “ I’m just wondering what changed — people change their mind, I’m just wondering what changed.”

STEVENS: “ This is about Abdul getting angrier and angrier and saying I don’t want these people in my campaign.”

COOPER: “ But he didn’t get angrier from midnight to this morning, something changed your mind — was there a soporific aspect?”

STEVENS: “Well, Anderson, you certainly weren’t on the phone with me at midnight.”

As Aaron Rupar put on X, this was a “seemingly mental breakdown.”

She could not explain the change in perspective and point to specific things besides “anger” she says Abdul El-Sayed has without describing what that anger is and how it showed up in the past 48 hours that made her change her mind.

Stevens was backed by Chuck Schumer during the primary. Folks were upset with Schumer for his hesitancy on supporting El-Sayed after the primaries. But after Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, Schumer called the move a “despicable betrayal.” Hakeem Jeffries and other Democratic leaders have also rallied behind El-Sayed, reaffirming their support for the party’s nominee. So her decision has the opposite effect that she intended.

The party that has spent months wrestling with internal divisions is now presenting a much more unified front around one candidate — the candidate she has pulled support from.

Whether this changes votes tonight remains to be seen. But Stevens’s decision has certainly changed the conversation and, unexpectedly, brought Democrats together around Abdul El-Sayed.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: DeSantis: War in Iran ‘big, big drag’ on Republicans
articles.summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said the Iran war is a “big, big drag” on Republican candidates this midterm cycle. DeSantis joined sports and political commentator Stephen A. Smith on SiriusXM on Monday night and said the Iran war and the high gas prices it has led to have hurt the GOP. A former…
articles.body:
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said the Iran war is a “big, big drag” on Republican candidates this midterm cycle.

DeSantis joined sports and political commentator Stephen A. Smith on SiriusXM on Monday night and said the Iran war and the high gas prices it has led to have hurt the GOP. A former challenger to President Trump in 2024, DeSantis has repaired his relationship with the president and campaigned alongside Republicans throughout the 2026 cycle.

“We just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact,” DeSantis said.

Gas prices hit a record high for an Election Day on Tuesday, reaching an average of $4.11 per gallon. Elevated prices are mostly due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for global oil transport.

The strait has been a key negotiation point for the Trump administration as they have tried to resolve the war, and while more oil is flowing than at the start of hostilities, prices remain high. DeSantis warned Republicans against ignoring the realities of the war’s impact on prices.

“If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them, and they’re not going to listen to you on other things,” DeSantis said.

The Florida governor said Trump ran on a platform of no new wars, and with an extended war in Iran, some GOP voters have “checked out.”

DeSantis added that the war could make 2028 difficult for Republicans if it lasts until the end of Trump’s term.

“If it drags on for the rest of his presidency, it’s going to be devastating to his ability to get anything done, and it is going to be very, very difficult for Republicans in the next cycle,” he said.

Asked what policy Republicans will reform their stance on if they lose on Tuesday — whether Trump supports it or not — DeSantis said they should shift their stances on artificial intelligence, data centers and Big Tech as a whole. He said if the Democrats are on “offense” on the AI issue, they will be able to attract voters who are historically more conservative.

“We do best as a party when we are standing for small business folks, people that are working hard,” DeSantis said. “When we get into corporatism, that’s when you really start to lose people.”

articles.title: Jon Stewart mocks Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech at Reflecting Pool
articles.summary: Comedian Jon Stewart mocked President Trump on Monday night for spending much of his final speech before the midterm elections discussing repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. On Monday’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Stewart ridiculed Trump’s decision to focus on the Reflecting Pool’s controversial, multimillion-dollar renovation shortly before voters would decide who will…
articles.body:
Comedian Jon Stewart mocked President Trump on Monday night for spending much of his final speech before the midterm elections discussing repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

On Monday’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Stewart ridiculed Trump’s decision to focus on the Reflecting Pool’s controversial, multimillion-dollar renovation shortly before voters would decide who will have control of Congress.

“That was the president of the United States on the day before the midterms choosing to make a speech at the Reflecting Pool to talk about the Reflecting Pool,” Stewart said.

“No symbolism, no metaphors, just straight-up pool maintenance,” he added. “That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech, if you will.”

Trump delivered his election-eve remarks Monday against the backdrop of the Lincoln Memorial, where he spent more than 20 minutes describing renovations to the pool, including repairs to cracked granite, pipes and the pool’s surface.

Stewart began his monologue by playing a clip of Trump touting his accomplishments since returning to the White House.

“I’ve kept every single promise I made, except far more. I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made,” Trump said.

“That is not possible dimensionally in this realm,” Stewart said in response. “That, now, dementially, yes, that that may be possible, but not dimensionally.”

The late-night host then pointed out the historical significance of the location, invoking similarities to Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, delivered from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

“In the shadow of the Lincoln Memorial with the echoes of Dr. King’s ‘I Have a Dream’ speech, please lay out for the American people what you think is most important for them to know,” Stewart said.

Stewart then played a montage of Trump detailing the restoration work, including the pool’s new paint and repairs to its surrounding stonework. When the montage ended, Stewart abruptly walked offstage before returning moments later, appearing bewildered by the president’s remarks.

images.caption: Host Jon Stewart is seen on the Comedy Central series “The Daily Show” on July 27, 2026, in New York.

articles.title: DHS’s Mullin warns people who illegally vote will be hunted down
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin is warning noncitizens not to vote in the midterms, saying the department will “hunt down” any who cast ballots. “If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, @DHSgov will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin is warning noncitizens not to vote in the midterms, saying the department will “hunt down” any who cast ballots.

“If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, @DHSgov will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” Mullin wrote on the social platform X . “Only American citizens should be deciding American elections.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shared a similar message on social media, writing, “There will be no escape.”

It is illegal for noncitizens to cast ballots in federal elections, though some localities and states allow noncitizens to vote in local races.

The Trump administration has made a forceful effort to remove noncitizens from voter rolls in the midterms, sending threatening letters to election officials and even taking some to court over a refusal to turn over their voter roll information.

The Department of Justice accused California of having more than 20,000 “likely noncitizens” on its voter rolls, a claim that has been disputed by outside analyses. A federal judge ruled the Trump administration had to stop threatening California election officials with criminal prosecution.

The DHS has repeatedly claimed that states, mainly Democratic ones, have thousands of noncitizens on their voter rolls. But there is no federal database containing a list of every U.S. citizen, and records can be inaccurate or out of date.

The New York Times reported in September that the DHS accused Nevada of having nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens on its voter rolls, a number that was revised down to 185. When Nevada officials investigated, they found that all 185 were U.S. citizens.

Multiple studies have found that noncitizen voting is not widespread in U.S. elections.

New Jersey did identify instances of noncitizen voting earlier this year, which was due to a software glitch. More than 6,000 were erroneously registered, but fewer than 400 actually cast ballots. The Garden State addressed the error once Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) was notified, the governor said.

Some Democrats and Trump critics hit back at ICE and the DHS for their posts warning noncitizens Tuesday. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) quipped that he would prosecute ICE if the agency showed up to the polls.

“If YOU show up to the polls illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you,” Newsom wrote back on X, matching the language ICE used. “There will be no escape.”

“Watch out!! ICE is gonna deport the literally dozens of people who do this,” former Rep. Adam Kinzinger (R-Ill.) replied on X.

The final voting of the midterms is underway, and the first polls close at 6 p.m. EST.

images.caption: FILE – Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials, speaks during a news conference at ICE Headquarters, Oct. 9, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

articles.title: Paxton: Review of Harris County voting claims ‘won’t be resolved by the time the election is over’
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton said the investigation into claims of felons voting in Harris County will not be resolved by the time “the election is over” on Tuesday. Paxton’s office announced Saturday it had arrested an undisclosed number of convicted felons who had voted in the midterms. The attorney general…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton said the investigation into claims of felons voting in Harris County will not be resolved by the time “the election is over” on Tuesday.

Paxton’s office announced Saturday it had arrested an undisclosed number of convicted felons who had voted in the midterms. The attorney general said Tuesday on Fox News the investigation won’t be completed by the election but that voters should know it is being addressed.

“My Election Integrity Unit is actively investigating additional reports of election crimes,” Paxton said in a press release. “We will continue working to protect the lawful votes of Texans.”

The attorney general’s office said the claims stemmed from a concerned citizen who filed a report and provided “open-source” information to support the allegation. In conjunction with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, Paxton’s office said, it confirmed the voter’s criminal status and made the arrests.

Whether a convicted felon can legally vote is governed by state law. In two states, along with Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, felons never lose the right to vote. In 24 states and territories, felons can vote once they are released from prison, 15 allow felons to vote once they are off parole or probation and 13 either never allow felons to vote or require them to finish their sentence and apply for their voting status to be restored.

In the Lone Star State, felons are eligible to vote once they have completed the entirety of their sentence, including parole or probation. A local news outlet reported Monday that two men had been arrested and confirmed their active status under probation.

“We’ll be pursuing this, it won’t be resolved by the time the election is over, but at least people will know that my office took care of election issues that were fraudulent or people voting that shouldn’t be voting,” Paxton said Tuesday.

articles.title: Trump Jr. invokes Charlie Kirk assassination in last-minute plea to voters
articles.summary: Donald Trump Jr., President Trump’s son, invoked the 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk in a Tuesday post urging voters to hit the polls before they close. Trump Jr. posted an image on social platform X of Kirk speaking to a crowd, appearing to be from the same Utah Valley University event during which…
articles.body:
Donald Trump Jr., President Trump’s son, invoked the 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk in a Tuesday post urging voters to hit the polls before they close.

Trump Jr. posted an image on social platform X of Kirk speaking to a crowd, appearing to be from the same Utah Valley University event during which the commentator was fatally shot. Text above the photo read, “Vote Like the Other Side Will Kill You for Talking.”

“Vote like your lives, and the lives of your children depend, on it. BECAUSE THEY DO!!!” Trump Jr. captioned the post.

Kirk, the Trump ally who co-founded conservative youth organization Turning Point USA, was fatally shot in September 2025 as he was speaking to a crowd of thousands in Orem, Utah. The assassination galvanized Republicans around the topic of political violence, with many — including the president — attributing violent rhetoric at the time to the “radical left.”

Republican candidates and lawmakers continued to use Kirk’s death throughout the year as an example of what they argued was the left’s propensity for violence.

During the second day of Trump’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, which overlapped with the first anniversary of the fatal shooting, the Republican National Committee included a memorial for the slain political activist. Speakers throughout the day slammed Democrats for their reactions to Kirk’s passing, echoing Trump’s remarks from the first day, in which he said, “The mask came off the radical left.”

“They mocked the attempted assassination of my father in Butler, Pa.,” Trump Jr. said during his remarks at the convention. “And we all saw the demented reaction from them to the sick coward who slithered onto a roof to assassinate our great friend Charlie [Kirk].”

Kirk was also a key player in Trump’s return to the White House last year, with the president saying, “No one understood or had the Heart of the Youth in the United States of America better than Charlie,” after the conservative activist died.

Trump Jr.’s post also comes as Republicans face a rocky path to holding on to power this midterm cycle, with the Iran war’s growing unpopularity, his father’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living weighing the GOP down.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, the president’s approval was sitting at 38.4 percent Tuesday afternoon .

Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, posted a video of her late husband Tuesday highlighting what she described as his “timeless wisdom” before polls close. In the clip, which she said was filmed before the 2024 elections, the conservative activist said, “I have no idea what will happen, but whatever happens, we’ll keep fighting.”

images.caption: Donald Trump Jr. speaks at a memorial for conservative activist Charlie Kirk, Sept. 21, 2025, at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz.

articles.title: North Carolina, Massachusetts, New York report technical issues at polls
articles.summary: Multiple states including Massachusetts, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and New York have reported technical issues at the polls on Election Day. Issues were reported with election machines in the city of New Bedford, Mass., but were eventually resolved, according to local news station WBSM. The city spokesperson, Jack Thuon, said there were issues reported in four…
articles.body:
Multiple states including Massachusetts, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and New York have reported technical issues at the polls on Election Day.

Issues were reported with election machines in the city of New Bedford, Mass., but were eventually resolved, according to local news station WBSM . The city spokesperson, Jack Thuon, said there were issues reported in four precincts Tuesday morning.

“An internal wire in the machines at these locations was found to be physically interfering with the port on the machine where ballots are fed,” Thuon said in the report, adding that the size of the ballot may have contributed to the issue.

The issue was resolved and the machine returned to its normal functioning after election officials adjusted the position of the wires.

During a press conference Tuesday, Kansas Elections Director Bryan Caskey said voting was disrupted for about 90 minutes at a location in Leavenworth County. The disruption happened after the location ran out of ballots around 8 a.m., according to information obtained by NewsNation.

About a hundred ballots were delivered to the location instead of a thousand, due to a clerical error. The issue has since been resolved, but Caskey said voters were turned away.

The North Carolina State Board of Elections approved a voting extension after reported technical issues at the Tabor City Courthouse in Columbus County and shorter extensions in Gates, Lenoir, Wilson and Hertford counties.

The extensions will delay posting of statewide results by 45 minutes, according to a post on social platform X by the State Board of Elections.

Voting hours were extended to 8:15 p.m. in Columbus County, 8 p.m. in Lenoir County, 7:55 p.m. in Hertford County and 7:45 p.m. in Wilson County.

Machine setup issues delayed the opening of polling locations at three different precincts in Pennsylvania Tuesday morning, according to the Chester County, Pa., website .

A petition for a 30-minute extension of voting hours at these precincts was granted; the precincts will be open to voters until 8:30 p.m. All other precincts in the county will close at 8 p.m.

In New York, voting machines across polling sites in Westchester County were facing issues Tuesday after ballot scanners stopped accepting votes. The issues started when polls opened at 6 a.m.

The county’s election officials instructed voters to continue filling out the papers, which will be placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags and will be secured and counted later.

images.caption: Voters cast their ballots in the Queens borough of New York on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026.

articles.title: Police arrest 17-year-old in deadly mass shooting at California mall
articles.summary: A 17-year-old boy has been arrested in connection with a mass shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California that left a pregnant woman dead and six other people injured.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) – A 17-year-old boy has been arrested in connection with a mass shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California that left a pregnant woman dead and six other people injured, authorities announced Monday.

The suspect was arrested Nov. 2 at a home in Suisun City, three days after the deadly shooting at the Solano Town Center mall in Fairfield, according to the Fairfield Police Department .

The teenager, whose identity has not been released because of his age, was booked on suspicion of murder and attempted murder.

Pregnant woman killed, six others wounded at Halloween store

The Oct. 30 shooting occurred around 8:30 p.m. at the Spirit Halloween store located at 1350 Travis Blvd., where shoppers were purchasing last-minute costumes ahead of Halloween.

Officers responded to reports of gunfire and found seven people suffering from gunshot wounds.

Investigators said the shooter entered the store, spotted someone believed to be the intended target and opened fire, striking that person and six others.

The suspect fled the scene before officers arrived.

Authorities identified the woman killed as 31-year-old Constance Hages, who was pregnant, according to information provided by her family.

According to the San Francisco Chronicle , police believe Hages was the intended target of the shooting, which may have stemmed from an earlier disagreement. However, no information was provided on how the teen and the victim may know each other or what their relationship may have been.

Six other victims, all males between the ages of 16 and 43, were transported to hospitals.

As of Monday, four remained hospitalized, including a 19-year-old man in critical condition. Three others, ages 16, 23 and 32, were listed in stable condition.

Two additional victims, ages 19 and 43, were treated and released.

Teen suspect arrested following investigation

Detectives identified the alleged gunman within hours of the shooting after reviewing surveillance footage from inside the Halloween store.

A school resource officer recognized the teenager as a former student, helping investigators establish his identity, the Chronicle reported.

On Monday, police located the suspect in Suisun City and took him into custody.

During a news conference, Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall revealed that the teenager had previously been involved in a shooting at Fairfield High School in 2025.

According to police, the suspect was charged in that case and spent several months in juvenile detention before being released.

“This event shouldn’t have even occurred,” Marshall said, criticizing California’s handling of juvenile offenders.

Marshall called for changes to California’s juvenile justice system in the wake of the deadly attack, Bay City News Service reported .

The suspect is believed to have acted alone, though investigators are examining whether anyone else may have been involved.

The Solano County District Attorney’s Office is reviewing the case, including whether Hages’ pregnancy could warrant an additional murder charge. Formal charging decisions had not been announced as of Monday evening.

The investigation remains ongoing, with assistance from the FBI, officials said.

Anyone with information about the shooting is urged to contact Fairfield police via email at email 1030mall@fairfield.ca.gov or by phone at 707-428-7600.

images.caption: A total of seven people were shot at a Spirit Halloween store in the Bay Area on Friday night, according to authorities. (Credit: KRON)

articles.title: Winchester vs. Colt: Idaho votes to designate a state gun
articles.summary: Along with voting on their next members of Congress and amendments to their state constitution, Idaho residents will also decide the state’s first official gun when they vote this Election Day. In observance of America’s 250th anniversary, Idaho legislators gave voters the choice of six different guns to serve as the state’s official firearm. The…
articles.body:
Along with voting on their next members of Congress and amendments to their state constitution, Idaho residents will also decide the state’s first official gun when they vote this Election Day.

In observance of America’s 250th anniversary, Idaho legislators gave voters the choice of six different guns to serve as the state’s official firearm. The ballot advisory question is not binding, but the state Legislature could make the decision permanent via future legislative action.

Voters will pick between four long-barrel guns and two pistols — including two Winchester brand models, two Colt models, the M1 Garand and a Remington. Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks (R) told the Idaho Statesman he researched and consulted with other legislators before deciding on the final six options.

“I like the term ‘iconic,'” Monks told the Statesman. “I thought a little bit more historical than necessarily what’s popular today.”

In a bill that first brought the question onto the ballot, the state House pointed to a deep history of firearms in the United States and Idaho, from armed citizen militias during the Revolutionary War to pioneers using rifles to hunt for food.

“The Second Amendment to the United States Constitution protects the right to keep and bear arms as a safeguard against tyranny and for personal security,” the relevant legislation reads .

Today, the legislation states firearms support the state’s hunting and recreational shooting industries.

“Idaho has built a strong tradition of responsible gun ownership while having one of the highest per-capita gun ownership rates in the nation,” it reads.

While only six guns are on the 2026 ballot, Monks told the Statesman legislators won’t be limited to what voters decide when it comes to selecting an official firearm. When asked about criticism surrounding the nonbinding nature of the ballot measure, Monks stressed the importance of firearms to American history.

“Obviously, without guns, there would be no America,” he told the Statesman. “We’d still be a British colony.”

images.caption: Commonly used rifles from the Revolutionary War

articles.title: Justice Department: Election Day monitors deployed to every state for first time
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Tuesday it is sending Election Day monitors to all 50 states. In a press release, the department said it will go through with “its largest monitoring effort in history” Tuesday, featuring “approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states.” “Election integrity…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Tuesday it is sending Election Day monitors to all 50 states.

In a press release, the department said it will go through with “its largest monitoring effort in history” Tuesday, featuring “approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states.”

“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” Department of Justice Civil Rights Division Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said in the release.

“I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D), whose county is listed among those the DOJ will monitor, shot back at the department over their monitoring plan, saying in a Tuesday statement “this is a baseless and dangerous attack from the Department of Justice on how states run their own elections and an attempt to intimidate voters into staying home.”

Last month , Attorney General Todd Blanche defended his department’s plan to send 1,000 election monitors to polling places for the midterms.

The federal government has monitored elections since the 1960s, and the DOJ will make sure federal law is being enforced properly, Blanche said on “Fox News Sunday” at the time.

“They’re not going to Republican states, they’re not going to Democrat states, they are going to every state to make sure our elections are carried out legally, fairly and appropriately,” he added.

Blanche went after Democratic lawmakers for “fearmongering” in asserting the department was attempting to intimidate voters.

Officials in several states have recently played defense against President Trump’s election fraud claims, as he has doubled down on them before Election Day.

Trump, in remarks to the country over the summer, claimed to have seen “shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure.” The president pointed to a 2020 Michigan voter registration case, also going after California, suggesting the Golden State’s mail-in ballots were “floating aimlessly.”

articles.title: Sullivan campaign, NRSC form ‘recount fund’ for Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) campaign and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), the campaign arm for Senate Republicans, have organized a “recount fund,” according to a Tuesday filing with the Federal Election Commission, the latest sign that Republicans are prepared to contest the results of the Senate election in Alaska if anyone other than the…
articles.body:
Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) campaign and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), the campaign arm for Senate Republicans, have organized a “recount fund,” according to a Tuesday filing with the Federal Election Commission, the latest sign that Republicans are prepared to contest the results of the Senate election in Alaska if anyone other than the incumbent wins.

“The NRSC is committed to ensuring every vote is counted fairly and accurately, in each and every state, and we will be ready for all contingencies, including recounts, should they be necessary,” said Joanna Rodriguez, an NRSC spokesperson.

Scrutiny over the Alaska Senate race is heating up even before the results are counted, as Sullivan fights to withstand a challenge from Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola. The New York Times reported last week a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot was recruited by operatives linked to national Democrats and Peltola’s campaign.

There are several ongoing investigations into that reported scheme, including at the state and congressional levels , although the practice is not illegal according to state law.

The Trump administration had already sought to dispute the results if the presence of the other Dan Sullivan caused the incumbent senator to lose, citing voter confusion. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a lawsuit the Department of Justice was pursuing to block the results on those grounds.

Sullivan told CNN he would accept the results .

articles.title: Pardoned Jan. 6 defendant charged with threatening to assassinate DC federal judges
articles.summary: A Georgia man previously convicted in relation to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, who was pardoned by President Trump, has been charged with threatening federal judges. An FBI affidavit shows that a man named Cleveland Meredith threatened Washington, D.C., federal judges with execution in a post to Facebook. “ALL J6 Federal JUDGES will be…
articles.body:
A Georgia man previously convicted in relation to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, who was pardoned by President Trump, has been charged with threatening federal judges.

An FBI affidavit shows that a man named Cleveland Meredith threatened Washington, D.C., federal judges with execution in a post to Facebook.

“ALL J6 Federal JUDGES will be EXECUTED!” Meredith allegedly wrote in April.

The FBI says it verified that the account was associated with Meredith’s phone number and email and tracked his internet access data to his area in Georgia.

Meredith was previously convicted of threatening to kill then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) on Jan. 6, accusations which he pleaded guilty to.

“MEREDITH admitted to driving across state lines into Washington, D.C., on the evening of January 6, 2021, while possessing a pistol, a rifle, approximately 2,500 rounds of ammunition, and 10 large capacity ammunition feeding devices,” the affidavit reads. “MEREDITH texted a relative who was in Georgia and told his relative that MEREDITH intended to ‘put a bullet’ in the head of then Speaker of the House, Nancy Pelosi.”

Since Trump pardoned more than 1,500 people convicted of Jan. 6-related offenses on his first day in office, several have been arrested or charged with other crimes, according to a Lawfare analysis from June. The report found that at least 97 had been arrested or charged with other crimes since the Capitol attack, at least 14 on sex crime-related charges.

Trump’s move to pardon the Jan. 6 defendants, specifically those convicted of violent crimes, drew backlash from both parties at the time. Before the pardons, Vice President Vance said in an interview that those who “committed violence” should not be pardoned.

A Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted nearly a month after the pardons found that 83 percent of Americans opposed Trump’s move to grant clemency to those who committed violent acts and 55 percent opposed his pardons for those convicted of nonviolent crimes. Just 14 percent supported the president’s decision.

articles.title: Warnock: ‘2028 could very well be theoretical’ if Democrats don’t win midterms
articles.summary: Sen. articles.body:
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) said in an interview released Sunday that he believed “2028 could very well be theoretical” if the Democratic Party does not win Tuesday’s midterm elections amid GOP attacks and potential legal battles regarding election results.

“Now, where is your head on 2028?” Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Warnock during an interview that took place at a restaurant in Atlanta.

“My focus is on winning the midterms,” the senator answered. “And I think if we don’t … 2028 could very well be theoretical.”

“I mean, look what this president is doing. He’s already attacking California. He’s already filed this ridiculous lawsuit in Alaska. And while I feel hopeful about Tuesday, we still don’t know what else he’s gonna try,” he concluded.

The first case Warnock is referencing is the lawsuit the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed against California officials that sought to set aside 20,000 ballots the department claimed were from noncitizens.

The Supreme Court rejected the administration’s argument in a one-sentence order that contained no explanation and had no noted dissents. California previously argued in lower courts that the DOJ’s efforts and the lawsuit were an attempt to disenfranchise legal voters.

The DOJ filed another case concerning Alaska’s Senate race that attempted to block certification if incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) loses against Democratic nominee Mary Peltola. The DOJ argued that the appearance of Daniel J. Sullivan’s name on the ballot would confuse Alaskan voters, siphoning votes away from the Republican senator with the same name, and accused Peltola’s campaign of recruiting the second Dan Sullivan.

A federal judge dismissed the administration’s case , ruling that it hadn’t shown how Peltola could rectify their concerns as ballots were already prepared for Tuesday.

President Trump told reporters that he would respect the results of Tuesday’s elections “if they’re honest elections,” adding in a Truth Social post that he was watching Minnesota’s Senate race for voter fraud.

This comment received criticism from national Democrats, particularly Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) who accused the president of “laying the groundwork” to “steal” the election.

“He’s blatantly laying the groundwork to steal an election if his chosen candidate doesn’t win… Minnesota will not take kindly to thinly veiled threats from a guy we’ve rejected three times (soon to be four),” Smith wrote on social media last week.

articles.body:
Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) says Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) did Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed a favor with her last-minute decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) over the Democrat.

“I think that Haley did Abdul a favor,” Crockett said during an appearance on an episode of “ The Breakfast Club .” She added that the events surrounding Stevens will give El-Sayed “a boost” in the elections.

“I think that Haley is done with politics or she’s decided she wants to be a Republican going forward,” the Democratic representative added. “We will see what happens when we get back into Congress next week about how the caucus decides to deal with this situation.”

Stevens on Sunday endorsed Rogers following an appearance at a Detroit church event. Her decision came after a feud with El-Sayed in the preceding days of the midterm elections, that stemmed from a political advertisement tying Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S.

Stevens released a statement saying El-Sayed did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

El-Sayed and Stevens were initially scheduled to make a joint appearance at an event Sunday in Detroit alongside Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.), but El-Sayed asked her to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her. On Sunday, Stevens made an appearance with Rogers instead.

Stevens’s decision to reverse her support for El-Sayed was met with widespread backlash from Democrats .

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s switch, telling reporters , “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton made a remark similar to Crockett’s about Stevens’s decision, saying during an appearance on CNN, “I don‘t think it‘s going to have much impact. In fact, if it has any impact, I think it will end up helping Abdul.”

Michigan’s Senate race has grown competitive in recent days, with nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ saying El-Sayed is “likely to win” the race.

Nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report also shifted its rating of the race from toss-up to “lean Democrat.”

articles.body:
Iowa Senate candidate state Rep. Josh Turek (D) said he voted for three Republicans when he cast his ballot Tuesday.

Asked whether he voted straight down the ballot for Democrats, Turek said he voted for Republicans Susan Miller for Pottawatamie County supervisor and Lea Voss for Pottawatamie County treasurer. The Democrat is locked in a tight race against Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) for a battleground seat that could decide Senate control.

“Susan Miller I voted for, I think she does an excellent job on the county board for supervisors. Voss I voted for, I picked one other as well,” Turek said in a video posted by local news outlet KCRG-TV.

Turek has worked to strike a moderate tone as he runs to take over for outgoing Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) in the upper chamber. A former Paralympic basketball player, Turek is trying to be the first Iowa Democrat to win a Senate seat in nearly two decades.

While the Senate candidate split his ticket between some local Republicans and statewide Democrats, some believe ticket-splitting — voting for a Democrat for Senate and Republican for governor, for example — could be a potential outcome for Iowa’s elections this year.

According to an analysis of election outcome probabilities by Inside Elections , Iowa has a 35 percent chance of electing a senator and governor from different parties. According to Decision Desk HQ, Hinson is narrowly favored to win the Senate seat, while the governor’s race is leaning in favor of Rob Sand (D).

Taking a page out of social media firms’ playbook, artificial intelligence firms are on high alert for Election Day amid the threat of misinformation.

The AI industry is facing pressure to ensure their products are feeding out accurate information to voters and aren’t being used for election interference attempts.

From training parameters to image generation limits to “election war rooms,” AI firms are watching out for AI misuse Tuesday evening.

The strategy follows that of Meta, which launched an election war room operation in 2018 to counter misinformation on its social platforms Facebook and Instagram.

articles.summary: A small aircraft that crashed in Florida on Sunday likely partially broke apart in the air before taking a nosedive, a federal investigator said Monday, according to The Associated Press. A business Learjet crashed just before 1 p.m. EST in Cresthaven, Fla., near Palm Beach, after departing from Austin, Texas, and was en route to…
articles.body:
A small aircraft that crashed in Florida on Sunday likely partially broke apart in the air before taking a nosedive, a federal investigator said Monday, according to The Associated Press.

A business Learjet crashed just before 1 p.m. EST in Cresthaven, Fla., near Palm Beach, after departing from Austin, Texas, and was en route to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The crash killed all nine people on board.

The jet burst into flames upon impact and left a wide crater in the ground. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has opened a probe into the deadly crash and is focusing on the weather conditions at the time that may have created a wider debris field for investigation, the NTSB said Monday.

The pilot of the aircraft first reported problems at about 35,000 feet, and investigators will look into what the weather conditions were at that altitude, the investigator told the AP.

Victims of the crash include Austin businessman Adam Robinson, 45, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children, ages 4 and 2, the Austin American-Statesman reported . Other victims include two friends of Robinson and Sharp as well as their nanny.

The pilots of the Learjet 60 were identified as Jeff Gregory, age 55, and the copilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, age 20, The New York Times reported .

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for prayers for the victims after the crash.

“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost,” he wrote in a post to the social platform X. “@FAANews & @USDOT are closely monitoring this crash and will share updates as we learn more.”

Concerns over plane safety have been on the rise after the high-profile midair collision at Reagan Washington National Airport in January 2025, which killed 67 people.

But a CNN analysis of NTSB data found that, as of June 2025, air travel was not less safe than in previous years, and the safety record has actually improved over the years. Air travel is still much safer than other forms of transportation, accounting for around zero percent of annual travel fatalities in the analysis.

One area where air travel does fall short is a shortage of air traffic controllers.

A report from the Government Accountability Office in early 2026 found a shortage of air traffic controllers despite increased applications, driven by government shutdowns and the pandemic. The FAA unveiled a new plan in May to mitigate the staffing shortage, aiming to expand education programs and hiring.

articles.body:
President Trump said he was forced to turn off Fox News Tuesday as he was watching the channel for election night updates because of a segment on “The Five” featuring liberal pundit Jessica Tarlov.

“I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” the president wrote on Truth Social. “Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I’ll be back later!”

Tarlov had moments earlier argued with comedian and commentator Greg Gutfeld over which issues matter most to voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, with the Fox News host insisting high gas prices and the cost of living were top of mind for Americans.

In response, Gutfeld, a staunch Trump supporter, argued voters would not support Democrats because they, as he said, support sex changes for children.

Tarlov is a regular progressive voice on “The Five,” one of Fox’s most watched debate programs, and frequently appears on the channel’s airwaves.

She frequently spars with hosts like Gutfeld and Jesse Watters and has drawn the ire of the president before.

Trump has had an on – again , off – again relationship with Fox for years, often sitting for interviews on the cable channel and hiring a number of its top hosts to serve in his cabinet.

The president and his allies have also attacked the network over its polling and news coverage during his second term, arguing the Rupert Murdoch-owned cable channel is not supportive enough of him and his agenda.

Watters, another top Fox host, telegraphed some pessimism for Republicans ahead of Tuesday’s midterms.

“I feel like I’m about to play a game that I know I’m going to lose,” Watters said just minutes before the spat between Tarlov and Gutfeld broke out. “I’m just trying not to get hurt. And getting hurt would mean you lose the Senate. And right now the Senate is very much in play, and it’s making me angry.”
