articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville predicted an “astronomical” Black turnout would drive Tuesday’s midterm elections amid election forecasters anticipating a “blue wave.” “When I look around at candidates in other places, I think the story” Tuesday night and Wednesday morning “is going to be Black turnout,” he said during a Monday appearance on MS NOW. “I…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville predicted an “astronomical” Black turnout would drive Tuesday’s midterm elections amid election forecasters anticipating a “blue wave.”

“When I look around at candidates in other places, I think the story” Tuesday night and Wednesday morning “is going to be Black turnout,” he said during a Monday appearance on MS NOW . “I think Black turnout is not going to be high. I think relative to the rest of the election available, it’s astronomical.”

“That is going to carry a lot more than people in Louisiana, Mississippi particularly. It’s going to matter in places like Texas, going to places in Michigan,” the Democratic strategist concluded.

This comes after Louisiana’s — a red stronghold — Senate race shifted in Democrat’s favor in October by election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball.

Crystal Ball analyst Kyle Kondik wrote Republican Julia Letlow “could be in a tighter-than-expected race” with her opponent, Democrat Jamie Davis, citing early voting data by Louisiana-based conservative pollster John Couvillon showing “excellent Black voter turnout.”

In Mississippi, attorney Scott Colom is seeking to unseat Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). His campaign gained traction in the weeks leading up to Election Day as analysts predict Black voters will help decide the state’s Senate election.

The Magnolia State has the highest share of Black voters in the country at 36 percent.

“African American voters tend to vote 90-plus percent for Democratic candidates,” Austin Barbour, a Mississippi-based Republican strategist, said. “If you’re down voting in Mississippi, you start out with a significant voting bloc, so it’s a turnout game as every election is.”

Hyde-Smith and Letlow are the favorites to win in projections by The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ), though Republicans in reliably red states have faced rising voter frustration with rising costs and tariffs against other countries, particularly Canada.

“When you go and tell everybody you’re going to get us out of wars, you’re going to drain the swamp, you’re going to cut gas prices, you’re going to do all of this, and none of that is occurring, people get frustrated,” Mississippi-based Republican strategist Hayes Dent expressed.

Democrats are looking to win in Senate races in Texas, Alaska, Michigan and Minnesota in the party’s effort to regain control of the upper chamber.

articles.summary: Presented by AstraZeneca {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story What’s on the ballot: Abortion, transgender care While affordability and health insurance costs have taken up much of the oxygen, voters in several states will weigh in on contentious health issues like abortion and transgender rights. © AP Photo/Rebecca S. articles.body:
What’s on the ballot: Abortion, transgender care

While affordability and health insurance costs have taken up much of the oxygen, voters in several states will weigh in on contentious health issues like abortion and transgender rights .

Transgender rights: Voters in four states—Washington, Nebraska, Arizona and Colorado— will consider proposals banning transgender student-athletes from competing on sports teams that match their gender identity.

Arizona already bans transgender student athletes, but the measure would increase the number of schools that the existing ban applies to; prohibit transgender students from using restrooms, locker room, showers not designated for their birth sex; no longer allow females or transgender boys to participate on a boys’ team.

Colorado’s measure also applies to boys and girls’ teams (most of the discourse around transgender student athletes involves a perceived threat from transgender girls or women).

A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

In Nebraska and Washington, the measures would apply to only girls’ teams. Nebraska law already prohibits trans students from competing in line with their gender identity; the measure would codify it into the constitution.

Washington’s measure would require all girls who want to play K-12 sports, regardless of if they are transgender, would need their sex verified by a physician through either genetic or hormone tests or an examination of her reproductive anatomy.

Missouri’s Amendment 3 would add language to the state’s constitution banning gender-affirming care for minors — something already illegal under state law.

Abortion access: In Missouri, the same anti-trans ballot measure would reverse another ballot measure passed just two years ago that added abortion rights language to the state’s constitution.

Unlike the law that was passed in the wake of the Dobbs decision in 2022, Amendment 3 includes limited exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies (birth defect or congenital disorder), and for survivors of rape or incest only up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Nevada and Virginia voters will also be voting to amend their respective constitutions to guarantee abortion access to the point of fetal viability or afterwards in cases to protect the mother’s life.

Virginia is the only state in the South not to ban abortion at or before 12 weeks of pregnancy.

Nevada already passed abortion protections in the last election, but state law requires the measure to pass a second time .

In Idaho, Proposition 1 would reverse the state’s abortion ban and allow for pregnancies to be terminated until fetal viability. Idaho currently bans abortions at any point in the pregnancy, with exceptions for cases of rape or incest that have been reported to law enforcement or to protect the life of the mother.

articles.title: Trump-backed Kentucky Republican wins House seat
articles.summary: Republican Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL and farmer, is projected to win in the race to represent Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District, a seat currently held by President Trump critic Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Gallrein, whom Trump endorsed, defeated Democrat Melissa Strange and libertarian Jeremy Todd for the seat.…
articles.body:
Republican Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL and farmer, is projected to win in the race to represent Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District, a seat currently held by President Trump critic Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Gallrein, whom Trump endorsed, defeated Democrat Melissa Strange and libertarian Jeremy Todd for the seat. The president had stumped for Gallrein in the weeks leading up to Election Day.

Gallrein led by 29 percentage points — 59 percent to 30 percent — with a small share of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 6:20 p.m. Tuesday.

Gallrein defeated Massie in the GOP primary back in May, securing the nomination with 54.9 percent of the vote to Massie’s 45.1 percent.

Massie has repeatedly butted heads with the president, backing war powers resolutions that would limit the president’s military actions in Iran, spearheading legislation to require the Department of Justice to release files related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and opposing GOP-backed spending legislation.

Gallrein, meanwhile, has supported advancing many of Trump’s priorities, including finishing the construction of the border wall, funding Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and ending what he describes as a “woke” agenda, according to his website.

“For the same reason I joined the service then, I joined for this campaign now – to serve these folks. When President Trump talked to me back on 17 October in 2025 and told me I needed to serve my district, the party, and my nation again, then I went home, thought about it, prayed on it. He asked me to do that, and then four days later, I declared on 21 October to enter the race…to serve these folks. They deserve that,” Gallrein told KET last month.

Asked by KET whether he would pledge blind loyalty to the president if elected, Gallrein said, “What I pledge allegiance to is the Constitution and the Lord.”

“If you look at the oath of the congressperson, and then also the officer oath that I took when I joined the military, as I said at 26 years old, there’s two things that I swear to: the Constitution and the Lord. Full stop. That’s where my loyalty is. And then, furthermore, to the people I serve, I answer to them. It’s as straightforward as that,” Gallrein said.
